subsubtopic: STATUS OF CERTAIN FEMALE EMPLOYEES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I wish to present a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. It arises from the fact that women who work for Air Canada are faced by a "male only" policy which prevents them from becoming pursers, even though in some circumstances they may be called upon to perform as acting pursers with none of the better pay, status and working conditions attached to the position of purser. In view of this unjustifiable discrimination I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather):
That this House direct the Minister of Labour, who has responsibility for the status of women, to introduce immediately the legislation creating a Federal Commission on Human Rights and Interests which was promised in the Speech from the Throne as the means of protecting women from discrimination.

subsubtopic: SHORTAGE OF FERTILIZER IN EASTERN CANADA-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that it will soon be sowing time and in view of the shortage and skyrocketing price of artificial fertilizers in eastern Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the government seriously consider asking the Canadian Transport Commission and the potash and artificial fertilizer producers to take action in order that eastern farmers can obtain sufficient supplies of this necessary product to maintain their farming production.

subsubtopic: SALES TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS-INTEREST RATES- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to consider immediately an urgent matter.
In view of the fact that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and the high mortgage interest rates underlie the prohibitive costs of construction, especially for people earning less than $10,000 a year, or about 30 per cent of the population, it is urgent that this government introduce legislation to eradicate once and for all poverty, unemployment and inflation. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That this House take immediate action to remove the 11 per cent sales tax and reduce the interest rate to 3 per cent.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO CONTROL MONOPOLIES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of very urgent necessity.
Considering the cost of living increase and the control exercised by some individuals on several sectors of the market, and considering also that control appears as a real spreading monopoly, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Rondeau):
That the matter be immediately deferred to this House in order to prevent, through specific regulations, monopolies from altering the play of free competition and contributing to destroy Canadian private enterprise within a relatively short time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS AND NUMBERING THEREOF
speechtext:
On today's order paper some 163 bills in the names of private members are standing for introduction and first reading at this sitting. The House will recall that for several years it has been the practice to introduce and give first reading in a group to all such bills by unanimous consent. I assume that today the House will be willing to follow what may be termed as the usual practice in regard to these bills.
In a preliminary way, it must be said that there is some concern in the mind of the Chair concerning a number of the bills standing for introduction. By way of example, the very first bill standing for consideration by the House is one in the name of the hon. member for Hamilton West. This bill came forward last year in the very same terms as it appears today for consideration of the House. At that time it was ruled out of order after considerable procedural consideration by hon. members. I mention this bill because it is No. 1 on the order paper and the hon. member

for Hamilton West may wish to give the matter some thought in the meantime. I considered that in fairness to him this should be mentioned. It may be that any further comments in that regard or with regard to other bills should be deferred until the occasion upon which these bills are first taken up during private members' hour.
In addition, it might be said that some difficulty has arisen in recent years with regard to the grouping of private members' bills with government bills. In order to facilitate the filing and reference to each class of bill it is proposed in future to begin the numbering of private members' bills at C-101. The traditional pro forma bill will continue to bear the number C-l. Government bills will then begin at C-2 and continue for the first 100 numbers. It is thought that all government bills to be introduced in this session can be accommodated within that range of numbers.
May I ask, then, whether there is unanimous consent that all public bills listed on today's order paper in the names of private members for introduction be deemed to have been introduced, given first reading, ordered to be printed and to stand for second reading at the next sitting of the House subject, of course, to subsequent examination as to regularity of each bill. Is the procedure to which I have referred agreed to?

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had a question for the Minister fo Consumer and Corporate Affairs but perhaps he will be here a little later. In the meantime I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance relating to the statement by the Prime Minister last week that the present position of the government is that funds that the oil producing provinces may receive from the federal export tax are not subject to equalization. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether, in these circumstances, he has any explanation for his assertion at the time the export tax or charge was debated in the House that these funds were subject to equalization and that, in fact, for the months of October, November, December and January some $25 million would have to be found by the federal government to equalize the portion of the export tax received by the producing provinces?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: My statement has to be taken in context, on the assumption that if equalization were due as a share of export tax revenues, then, of course, it would be paid. I have been advised by counsel that a share of revenues under the export tax is not subject to equalization under the statute and regulations.

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say the minister disappoints me. May I remind him that the statement he made in the House was not subject to any such qualification but was stated as the position of the government. May I ask the minister, without going beyond the bonds of decorum, why he said to me in the course of discussions relating to the charge for the months of February and March, and in seeking unanimous consent, that these payments would be subject to equalization?

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot explain any further than I already have. I have been advised that, under the law and regulations as they now stand, any sharing or division under the Export Tax Act is not subject to equalization.

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION

subtopic: PROPORTION OF EXPORT TAX PAYABLE TO OIL PRODUCING PROVINCES-APPLICATION OF EQUALIZATION

subsubtopic: RETAIL PRICE OF BEEF-GOVERNMENT INTENTION RESPECTING ACTION TO ROLL BACK PRICES IN APPROPRIATE CIRCUMSTANCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs would be in his place this afternoon, but in his absence may I direct my question to the Prime Minister. It arises from the statement made yesterday by the chairman of the Food Prices Review Board to the effect that retail beef sellers have not responded to the drop in wholesale costs by lowering prices. I want to ask the Prime Minister whether the government currently has before it consideration of any steps to rectify this situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Stanbury (Acting Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
subsubtopic: RETAIL PRICE OF BEEF-GOVERNMENT INTENTION RESPECTING ACTION TO ROLL BACK PRICES IN APPROPRIATE CIRCUMSTANCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be pleased to take note of this question for the minister.

subsubtopic: RETAIL PRICE OF BEEF-GOVERNMENT INTENTION RESPECTING ACTION TO ROLL BACK PRICES IN APPROPRIATE CIRCUMSTANCES
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but I thought I had addressed the question to the Prime Minister. May I have another run at the Prime Minister and ask him whether the government now has before it consideration of any plans to empower itself or any ministry of the government to intervene in order to roll back prices in appropriate circumstances?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: RETAIL PRICE OF BEEF-GOVERNMENT INTENTION RESPECTING ACTION TO ROLL BACK PRICES IN APPROPRIATE CIRCUMSTANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for missing the first question. I was checking about the presence of the minister. It appears that he has gone to Winnipeg where he is meeting with his provincial counterparts and is also addressing the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce. Very properly, the acting minister did take notice of the question on his behalf.
As to the second question, the answer is yes. The government is considering various ways in which it will be able to ensure that the process spelled out several months ago by myself will take place-in other words, what we do when the Food Prices Review Board has made a recommendation, has met with the industry, has found they are faulty and that they have refused to redress the situation, and it is then up to the government to act. I believe the hon. member is asking: Have we any plans along these lines? The answer is yes.

subsubtopic: RETAIL PRICE OF BEEF-GOVERNMENT INTENTION RESPECTING ACTION TO ROLL BACK PRICES IN APPROPRIATE CIRCUMSTANCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in asking my final supplementary question may I parenthetically urge the government to urge itself and the Food Prices Review Board to accelerate the process to which the Prime Minister has referred. May I now ask him how soon the House may expect an announcement by the government as to the specific steps?

subsubtopic: RETAIL PRICE OF BEEF-GOVERNMENT INTENTION RESPECTING ACTION TO ROLL BACK PRICES IN APPROPRIATE CIRCUMSTANCES
speechtext: Soon, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
That this House regrets that the government has not extended the March 31, 1974 deadline under the Veterans Land Act and calls upon the government to consider taking immediate steps to extend this deadline.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased, on behalf of my party, to move this motion today, even though I know that the vital question of the day is the uncontrollable increase in the cost of living which is affecting most Canadians. I am pleased to be given this opportunity because, sir, we have almost reached the deadline; in 19 days the government intends to phase out the Veterans Land Act.
You are well aware, Mr. Speaker, of the number of times that I, along with other members of my party and of other opposition parties, have tried by every means at my disposal to convince the government and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) to reconsider the phasing out of the act. May I mention that several colleagues in my party and in the other parties have collaborated on this issue. I have collaborated on a number of occasions with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in bringing motions before the House for just this purpose. My most recent attempt was made on January 11, just before the House recessed, when I moved a motion for the adjournment of the House, since I felt that this situation was an emergency one at that time.
In your reply, sir, you acknowledged the number of times on which I had brought up the issue and indicated that there would be other occasions in the new session when I could direct attention to the issue. You mentioned that several allotted days were set aside for such purposes. I have taken advantage of the present allotted day to raise this issue once more. You are well aware, too, of the number of ambiguous answers given by the minister, who did nothing more than leave the door open by stating that the matter was under review.
In his speech to the House last Thursday the minister literally slammed the door shut on any hopes that remained in the minds of veterans still qualified that anything would be done, when he stated, as recorded at page 305 of Hansard:
On January 11 last, as reported at page 9281 of Hansard,-
The minister was referring to the question I had asked.
-I stated that if I had sufficient information to make me think the deadline date should be changed I would so recommend to the government. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I have carefully considered all relevant representations and data, including that determined by the Royal Canadian Legion in the survey it conducted last December. I am unable to conclude that such a recommendation would be warranted or appropriate.
However, what he was really saying was that he has disregarded the many thousands of replies to questionnaires sent out by the Legion, I think the total is around

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
8,000, and the many resolutions submitted to him by national veterans' organizations on behalf of thousands of veterans, plus the countless letters he has received from individual veterans. I am surprised that this did not justify the extension of the legislation. If this is the basis for his decision, all I can say is that judging from the letters my party receives every day, there must be two national veterans organizations, one which writes to him and one which writes to me.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
These veterans organizations represent the majority of some 900,000 veterans still living in Canada. I cannot accept the suggestion that the decision was based on what the veterans want or on the advice they offered. I believe it must be based on some other factors. Our motion today reads very simply, and I quote:
This House regrets that the government has not extended the March 31, 1974 deadline under the Veterans Land Act and calls upon the government to consider taking immediate steps to extend this deadline.
I am sure many members of the House might wonder why my party, on its first allotted opposition day, has raised as a national concern one section of the veterans charter when such a matter might be relegated to a very low priority. I hope that my remarks will provide the answer to that question.
First, I feel it might be worthwhile to review the act. It was enacted in 1942 and consists of three parts. Under Part I, financial assistance, grants and loans may be provided to qualified veterans who desire to settle on land as fulltime or part-time farmers or as commercial fishermen.
Part II provides that any qualified veteran who is approved for a loan under the National Housing Act may receive financial and other assistance to build his own home, provided he assumes his own construction contract with a maximum ceiling of $18,000.
Part III makes available additional fully repayable loans to full-time and part-time farmers and fishermen at the time they are established under Part I of the act, and to those previously established under Part I and still have a subsisting contract with the director. At the same time, low cost group life insurance is available to assist in the repayment of a veteran's remaining VLA debt in case of death.
Under Part I, financial assistance may be approved up to $40,000 or 75 per cent of the security value of the land, whichever is the lesser amount, for basic herd livestock and farm equipment. One advantage is that under this part of the act, the first $6,000 is available at only 3Vi per cent and the remainder at the current rate which is presently 7 per cent. Under certain conditions there are other stipulations of varying degrees, including conditional grants. Similar conditions prevail for commercial fishermen with varying grants and/or loans depending on the circumstances.
Under Part II of the act, loans are available up to $18,000, repayable at the going NHA rate of interest. This section of the act was introduced to assist veterans of World War II and Korea to become homeowners, particularly those who because of the nature and location of their

employment could not be established on two or three acres of land as part-time farmers under the act and whose income was insufficient to meet payments on the cost of a home built by a regular contractor under the National Housing Act.
Under the regulations, it is required that a veteran applying for a loan under Part II must hold a parcel of land of one half acre. However, when a parcel of land does not contain this minimum and no other land is available to make up one half acre, this requirement is reduced by 20 per cent with the exception that those veterans who are in receipt of a 50 per cent disability pension may be exempted from this minimum acreage requirement.
Over the years amendments to the legislation were introduced, both with regard to the amount of the loan ceiling and the deadline dates for certification. For example, in 1965 the loan ceiling under Part II was raised from $12,000 to $18,000. This remains today, almost 10 years later. It must be pointed out also that deadline dates for certification were extended as a result of changing conditions. It was established in 1962 that deadlines would be introduced. October 31, 1968 was established as the deadline date for certification with March 31, 1974 as the date for applications for loans.
Today, there are over 100,000 veterans certified who cannot apply because of the restrictions of loan ceilings and lot requirements. Many of these veterans are still serving and are not ready to locate at a predetermined location. The minister keeps repeating, and his department reports predict, that a small percentage of the some
140.000	became certified in October, 1968 in case they may want to apply before the March, 1974 deadline. Nothing could be more far-fetched, Mr. Speaker. As everyone knows, the real reason is that with today's housing costs, it is impossible to build a home and provide a lot of over
17.000	square feet for $18,000. They actually do not get a loan of $18,000 since the down payment required is $2,600.
Purely and simply, governments past and present, even with their good intentions, failed to predict what changing conditions have brought about. I am sure the minister and some of his colleagues will use the argument that when the deadline was established, there was unanimous consent in the House and that it occurred during the time of the Progressive Conservative government. However, there were earlier deadlines established by other governments, and they were changed to meet increases in costs over the years or for other reasons. There have been countless amendments over the years to help cope with changing conditions, regardless of which party happened to form the government of the day, or who made the decision to impose deadlines. Therefore, why do they not admit that it is only fair and reasonable to extend the deadline, something which they have the power to do?
The main point I want to bring out is that the motion goes beyond the material advantages that would accrue to the veteran as his right. It is not wholly because the government has failed to increase the amount of the loan and amend the lot requirements. It is not merely because of the other factors I have mentioned. It goes beyond that. There is a principle involved here, not only an important principle but one which indicates a breaking of faith by the government of Canada which, in the name of every
March 12, 1974

citizen of Canada, made a commitment to the veterans of World Wars I and II and Korea.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
That commitment was made when the Prime Ministers of the day stated clearly and emphatically that no veteran, whether he remained where wars were fought or returned, would ever have cause to say that Canada broke faith with those who died, those who remained or those who returned.
Our motion today goes beyond the mere denial of the veteran's right under the Veterans Land Act. It brings into focus how easily we forget and points out the lack of recognition of what our country is all about. I am the first to admit that, in spite of the criticism by the opposition, myself included, as a country we are the envy of other nations of the world insofar as prosperity and freedom are concerned. How did we reach this state of affluence? We reached this status because we built a base of greatness through the initiative and dedication of the people who make up our citizenry. We also reached our status through the suffering of people who came to Canada because of the opportunities that existed.
We are made up of people of every race, and from all parts of the world, who were willing to participate in the building of a nation. They helped build Canada through sweat, toil and suffering. They were willing to suffer. When they were called upon during wars, they offered their lives to defend their country and to join with their neighbours to ensure peace in the world.
The minister also mentioned in his speech that this year would mark two important events for the veterans of this country. First, this coming June will be the 30th anniversary of the landing of the allied troups in northern France which resulted in the liberation of Europe and the end of World War II. He said the government, and rightly so, will take a very active part in the ceremonies. I am sure that all members feel the minister will be a worthy representative of our government and our country. Perhaps I can suggest he would be wise to include in his address an extract from the booklet entitled "Veneration for Valour, an assessment of the veterans charter and its impact on Canadian veterans and on Canada as a whole". I should like to read from this booklet. In it, we find these words:
How have we dealt with those who served and came back? They offered their lives as citizens of the Canadian nation, and they gave much. How have we dealt with the widows and orphans of those who did not come back? How did they expect to be repaid? The answer, in their name, was given by the Canadian Legion at its founding convention 46 years ago. Through all of those years the work of the Legion has involved, in the words of Senator Arthur Laing, Minister of Veterans' Affairs, "the awakening of the peoples' indebtedness, a sense of compassion for those who have suffered, and a veneration for valour." Its twin objectives, as defined by its first president, were "the welfare of Canada and the proper care of all who served their country in time of war.
It is well to note the priorities in those objectives. The welfare of Canada came first, the care of the veterans second. Yet both were linked together. They remained in the same order, and they remained linked, at the close of the second World War. There could never be a sound nation, a national at peace with itself, without adequate recognition of its veterans' claims. It must be just, but it must be feasible within the limits of our national resources. And what did that demand?
Veterans Land Act Extension
It demanded first, without thought of any limits, the generous care of the disabled; and that was always given. It was recognized in the years following the first World War as demanding a measure of help to all returning men. By the end of the Second World War, in a changing nation and a changing world, it had assumed a new dimension. Rehabilitation, both as a national obligation and as sound national policy, had come to mean helping the veteran to establish himself in civil life in a situation at least as good as he would have occupied if he had not gone to war. It was a large objective, pursued through a quarter century and still being pursued. Both in money and human efforts the work of the Department of Veterans Affairs represents one of our greatest national projects. It is a successful project, and a living force in the nation. In keeping faith with our veterans we have not only served them; we have joined with them in the building of a better country.
This may sound emotional, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps, when we stop to consider what is going on around us, we should get emotional more often.

speechtext:
In this same booklet, Mr. Speaker, a reference is often made to the Veterans Land Act, in particular to land settlement and home construction. The performance statistics show a large measure of success. Some 32,000 veterans have been settled on farms and
85,000	on small holdings. More than 36,000 have been assisted to build houses. The booklet goes on to say that these figures are of little help in themselves as a means of measurement, and that the work is not yet complete. More homes have yet to be built; more farms are being enlarged. So, I ask the minister this question; Why, when only a year and a half ago there was so much more to be done, should this work suddenly become unnecessary?
Let us turn for a few moments to the way in which the act has been administered, and look at a few of the statistics which the government uses so readily. Investment of public funds stands at present at $535 million. Total revenue received from veterans during the year prior to the publication of the report amounted to $69 million-$43 million representing new payment of principal, and $26 million representing interest payments. During that year some 2,100 loans were negotiated. House construction starts increased in Quebec and the Maritimes, remained steady in British Columbia and the Prairies but declined in Ontario, due mainly to rising costs and the difficulty of finding suitable land. The cost of new construction, alterations, additions and repairs amounted to nearly $80 million. Under the small holdings provision, the most popular form of assistance, some 3,000 veterans were established.
A staff of 536 is employed in the VLA administration. The annual report states that work production increased to 103.5 per cent relative to an index base of 100 for the year 1969-70. The administration, in addition to its other work, provides an appraisal service to other departments, particularly the Department of National Revenue, and in the year referred to completed almost 23,000 reports for that department's data bank. I wonder whether the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) has heard about that? So, here we find a competent administration working above the acceptable performance level, working for other departments, maintaining an acceptable business record. Yet the government has announced its intention of phasing it out.
27398-^28

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
How many amendments have we seen brought down in the past few years to the housing legislation for which the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and Housing (Mr. Basford) is responsible? How much money is being poured into this area? Certainly, everyone would agree that further vast amounts of funds must be provided for housing because of the housing crisis. But is there any reason or justification for phasing out legislation which is serving the veteran at no unreasonable cost to the public, particularly since doing so would have the effect of throwing thousands of veterans into the mainstream of the demand for housing which today is so acute?
The minister told us in his speech that he would be attending the biennial convention of the Royal Canadian Legion. Again, I say he will be a worthy representative. I am sure he will make reference to the increases effected in war veterans' allowances, civilian war allowances and in disability pensions. And so he should. I shall be proud, as will all members who played some small part in passing legislation to effect these increases. I am sure the minister will mention the fact that Canada's veterans charter compares with the best in the world, if, indeed, it is not the best. So he should, Mr. Speaker, and once again my colleagues and I will be proud to be associated with him.
But will it be fair to tell the 2,500 veterans who will gather from across the country at the Dominion command convention that after reviewing all the factors he was unable to conclude that the extension of the March, 1974, deadline was warranted or appropriate? I say it will not. I hope he will be able to sell them something along these lines-that the government, realizing the commitments made by past governments over the years are in the name of every Canadian citizen, has decided to continue to keep faith with its Canadian veterans and not only to extend the March, 1974 deadline but, as well, to extend the October deadline. Further, that it has decided to increase the maximum ceiling and reduce the lot requirement in line with today's needs, and that it will undertake to ensure that no veteran would be denied the right to acquire a home, or a small holding or to improve his home under the terms of the act as long as he lives.
As I said in my opening remarks, I have attempted over the past many months, with the support of my party, by questions in the House and in committee meetings, by way of motions, a private members' bill and other means, to persuade the government to reconsider its decision to phase out the act. I have attempted to do so in a responsible manner. Nevertheless, I understand there are rumblings going around that there are ulterior motives behind the motion we are putting forward today. All I can say is that I am sorry for those who think that way.
With only 19 days left before the phasing out of the legislation, the motion before us is a last effort of mine to appeal to the government to take steps to extend this deadline. It is a known fact that on matters concerning the veterans of Canada the members of this House have always stood together. This attitude has been exemplified from time to time on many occasions, particularly at meetings of the Veterans Affairs Committee. I am sure that all hon. members, some 50 of whom are veterans, appreciate the emergency which exists. I am sure, too, that all members of the House will support this motion, and, in

doing so, indicate that as representatives of every citizen in Canada we are fulfilling our commitments to the veterans of this country to whom we owe so much.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my first words I wish to commend the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for presenting this motion to the House today. I also wish to commend him most warmly on the clear and responsible manner in which he presented the case asking the government to reconsider the question of the deadline on the Veterans Land Act and to continue that legislation beyond the end of this month.
It has been my privilege-and I thank my hon. friend for having referred to it-to collaborate with the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) on a number of matters relating to veterans affairs. I should like to take this opportunity to acknowledge once again that he did me the honour of seconding the motion that I presented to this House on November 9, 1973, under Standing Order 43. That motion called for a reconsideration of the whole question of the Veterans Land Act. I shall refer to its terms in a few minutes, but I wish to emphasize the fact that unanimous consent was given to the making of that motion and that the House supported it unanimously.
That is perhaps one of the reasons, along with the others that he stated, for the tone in which the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe spoke this afternoon. He spoke not just for himself and for the members of his party, and I hope that I speak not just for myself and for the members of my party. I believe we are speaking for members in all parts of this House, and I am able to say that not just because of a personal judgment of what all hon. members think, but because there was unanimous approval of the motion that was made on November 9, 1973.
I realize that in a speech that he made last week the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) seemed to say that he had given this matter all the consideration that he could, and that he was not able to bring himself to continue the legislation. However, I join with my hon. friend, and with others who will speak after me, in making the strongest appeal I can to the minister. My appeal is that when he speaks in this debate today, as I trust he will, he will be the big man that all of us know him to be and will be prepared to say that, despite what he said last week, in view of the desire of the House he is now prepared to do what this motion asks, namely to reconsider the phasing out of the Veterans Land Act. I hope I can be pardoned for saying that if the hon. minister is already a hero, he will be a hero again today if he accepts and reflects the thinking of this entire House by stating that the time has come to make it clear that the Veterans Land Act will be continued beyond the end of this month.
If there were time I would recite events other than the motion of November 9. Questions were asked by my hon. friend from Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe and myself on November 21, 1973, which resulted in a late show on
March 12, 1974

Tuesday, December 4, 1973. There were motions and questions in January when we were back here for the end of the session. There were motions on Friday, March 1. The matter has been discussed at length at meetings of the veterans affairs committee.
Even though this question may be one of the lesser issues in the field of veterans affairs, it is before us now because of the deadline of March 31. It is also before us because of the feeling in all parts of the House that it is an issue on which the government should now respond to the will of the House, even though this means changing a position that the minister was very close to taking when he spoke in the debate on the address last Thursday night.
So, Mr. Speaker, that is my plea. I deeply appreciate the manner in which the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe made his plea. He was speaking the absolute truth when he referred to the way in which we get along in the veterans affairs committee and the way in which we deal with veterans affairs in this House. The last thing that we want today is partisan conflict, especially when we are all agreed.
I do not know when the minister will speak. If he wants to sit and listen to the debate before he answers, then that is fine with all of us. But I do hope he knows that in the hearts of all of us in this House we want a clear, unequivocal, good faith assurance today that this matter will be reconsidered.
Thanks to the speech of my hon. friend who preceded me, there are details about the legislation with which I do not need to take part of my 20 minutes to deal. However, I should like to make a few brief comments, and to support my comments by reading extracts from a letter, in regard to some of the arguments that the minister has been putting up when he has been resisting our wish that the Veterans Land Act be continued.
One of his arguments has been that the purpose of the Veterans Land Act has become confused in the minds of veterans in recent years. The minister has pointed out that originally the act was to assist veterans to get settled on a small holding of land on which they would do a certain amount of do-it-yourself agriculture. The minister says that what is happening now is that veterans are trying to get grants under the Veterans Land Act for the purpose of erecting a house for their retirement years.
The other night when the minister made that comment in his speech I interjected-and it is the obvious interjection-"What's wrong with that?" I remind the minister that the motion which was passed unanimously by this House and accepted by him, by all members of the cabinet and by members of all parties on November 9 dealt with that very question. These were the words of the motion, as recorded at page 7693 of Hansard:
That this House requests that the Minister of Veterans Affairs give urgent consideration to the amending of the Veterans Land Act regulations to permit veterans to acquire small holdings, even if the main purpose of most of the older veterans now applying for loans under the Veterans Land Act is to meet their housing requirements, it being the view of this House that entitlement to a piece of this land ought to be the right of any veteran.
At the risk of repeating myself over and over again, that motion was passed unanimously by this House on Friday, November 9. The entire cabinet concurred in it. Surely, the
Veterans Land Act Extension
cabinet is not going to go back on what it agreed to do at that time, namely reconsider the whole matter, and to include in that reconsideration the justification that veterans have in seeking grants under the Veterans Land Act, even if housing is the main or the only purpose they have.
I remind hon. members, and I remind the government, that with housing costs as they are today some assistance is necessary. I ask hon. members, what group can this parliament more justifiably assist in the matter of housing than our older veterans? Really, Mr. Speaker, there is no answer to this plea: the government cannot say no. The government really has to come through today and agree to the request in this motion, which is that it reconsider the deadline placed on the Veterans Land Act.
Another argument the minister has used has been the assertion that some veterans were trying to get more than one of the various post-war benefits which were available to them. If I had the time I should like to develop that point myself, but I think the easiest way to deal with it is to read a part of a paragraph from a letter written to the minister on January 28, 1974, by Mr. E. V. Heesaker, Dominion President of the Canadian Corps Association. This was a letter in which a strong, and I think very effective appeal, was made to the minister to wash out the March 31 deadline.
Mr. Heesaker in his letter referred to the comments made by the minister in reply to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) on November 6, 1973 about this effort to get extra benefits, and he said:
We would like to point out here that there were many veterans who were not aware of the Veterans Land Act or the University Training Program until after they had used up all their re-establishment credits. And, of course, they had to refund their re-establishment credits before they could become eligible for Veterans Land Act Benefits. So they were not trying to take advantage of two forms of rehabilitation, they were merely changing one for the other after they had learned of the existence of Veterans Land Act.
I think the argument the minister is trying to make in that connection just does not stand up, and even if it did stand up, as I shall suggest by a sentence from Mr. Hee-saker's letter a little later on, I suggest our duty to those who served is such that we should not quibble over this sort of thing. Therefore, the plea today for the Veterans Land Act to be continued is one that should be met.
As I have already said, and as my friend who preceded me said, there are many issues affecting veterans in respect of which we want improvements, and we will keep up the battle for them. I agree with my friend that we have done pretty well in the last couple of years, but this happens to be an issue which is crucial as March 31 is only 19 days away.
Another argument the minister uses at times, and really it startled me that he would use it at all, is that it would be unfair to former veterans who did not get this benefit to give it now to today's veterans under different terms. That would be like saying we should not be paying old age security pensions of over $100 a month today at age 65 because that is unfair to our parents and grandparents who back in the thirties got only $20 a month at age 70.

speechtext:
My friend from Edmonton refers to increases in disability pensions. What about the veterans who have died over the years since World Wars I and II on disability pensions at much lower rates? Is it unfair to them that we now pay better disability pensions to those who are alive today? Really, I think that argument is one that the minister would like to reconsider. What we are concerned about are the veterans who are alive today, and if those who have died before them whether on the field of battle or since the war, could speak they would say they would like to see their comrades get the best of what is coming. This is a different society with more affluence and greater costs, and I suggest it is completely unfair to judge what is done for veterans today by what was done for veterans in days gone by.
Another argument the minister has used is that many of the hundred thousand to whom the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe referred, who got their certificates of qualification before the cutoff date in 1968, were just taking the precaution of getting their authority in case they wanted to use it. The minister says we should not now take those people seriously because they really did not mean it, but just wanted to be sure in case.
In answer to that I should like to read again a paragraph from the letter that Mr. Heesaker wrote the minister on January 28. He said, addressing himself to the minister:
You say that you are satisfied that the vast majority of veterans who hold Veterans Land Act qualification certificates simply took the precaution of obtaining such a certificate before the deadline of October 31, 1968. This is just like the precaution they took in 1914, and again in 1939, to ensure that no enemy soldiers set foot on Canadian soil, except as a prisoner of war. However, they were not so cautious with their own personal safety.
I suggest that is not the kind of argument that should be made in this debate, that many of these veterans were only taking a precaution. The fact of the matter is that times have changed, problems in gettting housing have become very serious, and in my view we should treat seriously the fact that many of these veterans who have these qualification certificates would like to be able to get themselves located on a piece of land for a home, even if they are not able to do so before March 31. As a matter of fact, I like the sentence in the concluding paragraph of Mr. Heesaker's letter in which he states:
In view of the above facts, we believe that a veteran should be eligible for benefits under the Veterans Land Act until the day he dies. He offered his life in a time of crisis and this is little enough to give him in return.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the motion introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), calling upon the government to extend the deadline under the Veterans' Land Act.
March 12, 1974

I share the interest of all previous speakers in this matter, for I am one of those who served our country during World War II, a war which was believed to be the very last of all major conflicts.
On a number of occasions, and especially during the past few months, similar motions were introduced calling upon the government to disregard the deadline which had been unanimously agreed upon in 1968 and to extend the benefits of this act later than March 31, 1974. On November 6, 1973, a similar motion was introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and another on December 4, 1973, by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe. These two motions, Mr. Speaker, were received with many reservations. I remember the debate that followed the motion, the kind that can be termed a "motherhood" motion. It is very difficult to object to the government paying increased benefits to those Canadians, who are first-class citizens because they took the responsibility in the difficult years of 1939 to 1945 of enrolling, going into training and defending their country.
Mr. Speaker, before developing further my ideas on this motion, I would like to return to the spirit of the act adopted in 1942. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will read from the preamble or interpretation of the act. I quote:
In this Act
"veteran" means a person who at any time during the war declared by His Majesty on the 10th day of September 1939 against the German Reich and subsequently against other powers, has been therein engaged on active service in a naval, army or air force of Canada, or of any of His Majesty's forces if at the time of his enlistment he was ordinarily domiciled or resident in Canada,
It can be immediately gathered from this preamble, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of the act was to favour those young Canadians who answered the call to arms and decided voluntarily, after being called, to go defend their country. The government of Canada has therefore taken very definite obligations towards them.

Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence I should like to read some of the notes in the preamble to the act entitled "An act to assist war veterans to settle upon the land".:
Whereas many men now serving in the active forces of Canada have recorded their desire to settle on land or engage in farming when hostilities cease, and it is desirable that suitably qualified veterans be encouraged to seek rehabilitation in the agricultural industry;
And whereas part-time farming coupled with other employment is an increasingly important aspect of rural and semi-rural life in Canada;
And whereas it is in the public interest as a measure of rehabilitation to assist in acquiring the ownership of farm homes by qualified veterans .. .
And whereas the great majority of prospective veteran settlers have limited financial assets and the lack of such assets has proved to be the main obstacle to the fulfilment of settlement contracts and to the acquirement of farm home ownership;
And whereas it is the purpose of the Dominion Government to provide a measure of financial assistance to veterans on their performance of prescribed settlement conditions in order to promote their engaging in agricultural pursuits either as a full-time occupation or as a part-time occupation coupled with some other employment:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the title of the act and the preamble clearly set out the purpose and intent of the legislation drafted by the framers of the legislation and
Veterans Land Act Extension
adopted by Parliament over 30 years ago. The reason I go back to the spirit of the law in 1942 is simple. During those days, of course, we had to create some incentive for, or some interest on the part of, young Canadians to join the service, to abandon careers, leave their families or wives or leave their studies in order to enter the service of their country not knowing whether they would come back or not knowing in what condition they would come back. Of course, the Canadian government took upon itself the task of preparing a program so that the experience of going over and fighting for their country would not deprive young Canadians, of whom I was one, of a career or business to which to come back. If there were no career or business to which to come back or studies to pursue, then if they wished to settle on a farm they could do so with the assistance of the government.

Mr. Speaker, this makes me wonder whether we are not somewhat stretching the spirit of the law. If, for instance, the benefits were increased or, for instance, the government, on the recommendation of the minister, were to recommend that in fact extension of the application of the act be studied seriously, I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether as a veteran who made his option some 27 or 28 years ago, I would not feel that I was being cheated in some of my rights because at that time I was not told that in 1974, following the representations of some veterans, the government or Parliament would consider extending the benefits of the act.
I wonder if my decision would have been the same in 1945, had I then known that, much later, I could change my mind. In any event, we must not forget that 100,000 veterans have already taken advantage of the act. Out of these, 48,500 who are still committed live on these tracts of land and are repaying their loans.
Of these 100,000 no fewer than 40,000 have already bene-fitted from the grant or benefits and finished paying their debt. Mr. Speaker, I wonder what attitude, and I urge my colleagues to think very seriously about this, those who have already made their decision could have. I wonder whether they will not have the very justified feeling of having been denied their rights by accepting benefits which could have been much more interesting had they waited like a few thousands have done.
This is a most indeterminate number considering that today as many as 48,500 are still committed concerning their land, and considering also the age of these veterans. I consider myself as one of the younger veterans, and yet I celebrated my 50th birthday in September 1973.
So, my information is that the present average age of veterans, as described in the original act of 1942, would be 55.
I believe that when I reach 55 I shall probably have behind me a good many of my productive years, and it is not at that age that I shall consider settling down on a farm.
Perhaps you are right. Some of my colleagues say with a smile that I have many more years to go. They are very kind to smile in the expectation that I shall still be here for a few years. It is probably the military service that kept me so young, Mr. Speaker, Nevertheless 55 is not an

age to think of going into farming or building a house, because one must not forget that this act was originally meant to help the veteran contribute to the building of his house. At the same time, he was committed to farming some of the time.
In any case he had a commitment. I recall reading this commitment and considering it very seriously. However, I was reviewing that act, Mr. Speaker, at an age when one enters a new career, that is at 24, 25 or 28 years. When I refer to the average age of veterans as being 55, it means that most of them are over 55. I wonder if they are taken in consideration when one asks that the benefits of the legislation be extended beyond March 31, 1974. Those citizens have already had 30 years to consider settling on a piece of land or an adequately large lot to make a living.
I do not know whether I was overly eager to select my profession when I decided not to settle on a farm after my release from the armed forces. Mr. Speaker, I know that many veterans 55 years of age or over are seriously considering farming. However, to draw some allowances under the Veterans' Land Act, veterans must undertake to pay a 25- or a 30-year mortgage. Therefore, if the average age of most veterans is 55 it means that a significant number of them are 60 or over. Is it possible to spend still 25 or 30 years on some land and build a home that late in life?
I have serious reservations about the motion introduced. However, I am keeping an open mind on the possibility of extending the application of the Veterans Land Act.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I take part in this debate on the motion put forward by the Progressive Conservative party.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the act referred to in this motion did not meet the legitimate aspirations of our brave soldiers. Naturally, an ill-conceived act is an obvious reason for nobody wanting to take advantage of it, to the point where Canadian veterans did little or nothing to avail themselves of the act. According to my calculations about 1 per cent of veterans saw fit to do so.
It is also obvious in these times, Mr. Speaker, that an amount of $18,000 is absolutely ridiculous when one considers that, because of taxes on building materials, prohibitive interest rates and inflation, the cost of construction nowadays is clearly too high to provide those brave soldiers with a decent house where they could spend the rest of their lives.
From a practical point of view, the act should be more comprehensive for those brave citizens most of whom gave up the nicer days of their youth and their dearest hopes in the madness of the last two wars.
Yet they had been given high hopes and promised a nice future upon their return. Unfortunately, faced with all sorts of obstacles, rebuffs and misunderstandings, they soon lost their illusions.
Judging from the speeches made by other members it seems there was an oversight in the act to provide those veterans with second mortgages while allowing them to build larger houses to accommodate a tenant in order to help them meet their obligations.

Furthermore, it seems the size of allocated lots was often out of proportion with the bylaws of municipalities or cities where they wanted to settle.
Of course it is quite difficult to draw practical conclusions from this motion since it does not bring anything new and simply perpetuates a situation which is absurd since the provision of the act is ineffective. The best evidence is that hardly one per cent of our veterans have taken advantage of this right.
Our government should certainly act in a more humanitarian way for all those brave citizens who are at grips with hardships resulting from the fact that they wanted to defend our freedoms. We suggest that the application of this legislation should be extended and the act amended to give more discretion and freedom to those concerned with veterans so as to satisfy their claims in the best and quickest way.
Let us not forget that the last amendments to the Veterans Land Act were made over thirty years ago. I believe that in 30 years, an individual or even a government is entitled to change his or its views to meet the requirements of the moment. It is obvious that thirty years ago, the veterans' needs were not the same as today. I think that this government should amend the act, maintain it and extend its application so as to do justice to all these brave soldiers who, as I said earlier, sacrificed their youth to defend our freedoms. We all know that nowadays, like most of our fellow citizens, they have difficulties finding a suitable shelter.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude my comments and ask whether it would be possible to preserve the present act and to amend it not so as to spoil our veterans, but in such a way as to be more human towards their claims and to understand that these people have made many sacrifices. Most of them lost their lives on battlefields. I think that at the same time we should have a special thought for veterans' widows and children who often suffer from our lack of gratitude and appreciation.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I hope that every one of us will do his utmost to ensure that the amendment we shall bring to the act will satisfy all Canadian veterans.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate to present the views of the 11 Legion branches, and army, navy and air force units in my area. The motion is a short, direct one, simply calling for the extension of the March 31 deadline for the Veterans Land Act.
When beginning these remarks I would like to look back to 1917 when the then Prime Minister of Canada addressed the Canadian forces on the eve of the great battle of Vimy Ridge, during which Canada became a nation and her troops were recognized throughout the world. It was Sir Robert Borden, speaking to the troops on that occasion, who said:
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and your courage is brought to the notice of your people at home.
Veterans Land Act Extension He ended by saying:
We will do these things so that no man will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken faith with the men who won and the men who died.
I believe those words, used in that situation, had the impact of a solemn obligation and sacred promise, not only to the veterans of world war I but to those of world war II and of the Korean war. Veterans throughout Canada, and indeed members of this House, are perturbed that the government seems bent on cutting back and ultimately phasing out the Department of Veterans Affairs. It is starting with the Veterans Land Act, and the cutoff date which is being debated today is one of the biggest steps towards the ultimate elimination of the work that act is able to do for the veterans of Canada. As I say, we are disturbed about this and so are the veterans.
The basic argument today is on whether or not to extend that deadline, and from it flows two things. If it is extended, then an extension can be sought of the ceiling with respect to grants given to veterans to build houses or buy property, to make that ceiling more realistic at the present time. The second factor related to this extension governs the lot size stipulated in the act, which is presently half an acre and which, under special conditions, can be reduced by 20 per cent. This could be modified so that veterans could take advantage of the VLA act to purchase city lots.
These two factors are the main reasons that many veterans have not come forward to take up contracts, even if they have been certified as being able to do so. When the minister says that very few veterans have come forward to take advantage of this program it is because of the discouragements and roadblocks that these two factors represent. The failure of the 150,000 veterans who established eligibility to take out loans is the direct result of these two major difficulties.
Pertaining to this date of March 31, 1974, we must remember there was the decision made first establishing a termination date of October 31, 1968 for qualifying for these loans. This date would also have to be altered if we can persuade the government to change the March 31 date. As envisaged, all lending under the VLA act will cease on March 31, 1977. I mention the lot size requirement and the ceiling because these, fundamentally, are tied in with the extension of this deadline.
That veterans are concerned about this issue is shown by correspondence which has come across the desks of all members of parliament. I will read one extract from one letter sent by a veteran who lives in Simcoe, Ontario. Mr. Wilfred Lauzon said in his letter:
I am a pensioned veteran, drawing a disability pension and also a holder of a VLA contract. I am interested to see the deadline extended beyond the date of March 31/74 ...
He said that he would like to see the loan ceiling raised as well. He then said that he had talked to other veterans who are interested in seeing the deadline extended, and that they had filled out the questionnaire which was referred to earlier this afternoon by the mover of the motion in his opening remarks. I commend the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall)

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
for his speech and for the compelling arguments he raised for extending the deadline.
I think the minister and the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs have argued on various occasions that we are merely making house lots available to veterans. When the Veterans Land Act was first passed it was meant to provide small holdings for veterans. This was to enable them to become part-time farmers. Some of them, no doubt, became full-time farmers. As I say, that may have been the original intent of the act. Conditions today are materially different from those existing at the time the act was first passed and when men first obtained benefits under it. We are now in a totally different ball game. I do not see any earthly reason why the Veterans Land Act cannot become a vehicle for providing a means of easing the housing shortage which is being felt across this country.
I could say more, but I do not want to repeat what has been said. I will conclude by telling the House why we, on my side, have moved the motion and why we think all members of the House will support it. First, if the deadline is not extended, 100,000 veterans will be denied their rights under the Veterans Land Act. I am speaking of those men who have been certified as eligible for benefits. Second, the act can become an important vehicle for fighting the acute housing shortage in this country. Third, the motion gives an opportunity to all members who so wish to participate in this debate and present arguments which may further convince the minister of the necessity of doing what we propose. Fourth, and equally important, by means of this motion we will strengthen the hand of the minister. Basically, I feel that if the minister alone had the power, he would decide in favour of doing what we ask. I know he has to persuade the other members of the cabinet that this is a good idea. I hope, as a result of our debate today and the arguments which have been and will be advanced, his hand will be strengthened when he is dealing with the other members of the cabinet, so that the government will see there is widespread support for the motion we are now proposing.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having heard the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I suspect that they are as good as if the government had spoken. I cannot bring myself to believe that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would have gone that far out on a limb in expressing his own opinions and risking the defeat of the government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext: Don't be too sure.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
It is with considerable pride that I participate in this debate. I begin by congratulating the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe for the motion which he introduced earlier.

This motion is put before the House at the right time because it is aimed at getting justice for those who served

their country. Personally I have not had the privilege of serving in the armed forces; this is why 1 try to compensate by serving in politics, although it is perhaps not comparable. I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that I often have the opportunity, in my constituency and particularly in Saint-Hyacinthe and Ottoburn Park, to meet members of the Canadian Legion and appreciate what they do in the community and their activities.
I am proud to pay tribute to them in this debate and to underline to what extent their contribution is necessary to the progress of Canadian society.
I take part in the debate at this moment because the most elementary fairness requires the extension of the deadline under the act, in order to enable those who fall under its jurisdiction to defend their rights.
To begin with, Mr. Speaker, it is a question of gratitude from the Canadian people and particularly from parliamentarians towards veterans. We must remember-and not only on Remembrance Day when with much noise and pomp we pay tribute to those who gave their lives and made tremendous sacrifices to protect their country. This memory must be externalized, manifested, translated in to acts and gestures which have significantly more value and meaning than the words that can be said in front of a memorial each year in November.
I recall that I was deeply moved last year when listening in this House to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe on the 29th anniversary of D Day. We were then paying tribute to our soldiers who took part in the allied landing in Normandy. Veterans remember the events that took place on French beaches 29 years ago and they remember their brothers in arms who fell at their sides, those who were not fortunate enough to come back to Canada and reap the benefits offered by as prosperous and promising a country as ours.
It is significant, Mr. Speaker, that we should have to recall that 29 years ago that crusade was being undertaken in the name of national unity and that nowadays national unity is still the main objective, an issue from one end of this country to another, the objective we are trying to achieve through our speeches as well as our legislative measures. But alas, we do not realize that this country has grown up and that we owe it to thousands of our young fellow citizens, including a good many-and I am privileged to sit next to them-who are members in this House. As volunteers in 1939 and 1945 they went to fight for their country to protect Canada and the free world against other nations' voracity and thirst for power. They fought together irrespective of race, religion, colour or origin. They fought together as Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, we can keep on building a still more splendid country if we take the trouble to look back on the past and draw our inspiration from that spirit of comradeship created among our veterans through the suffering they shared on battle fields, a comradeship that will stay at the bottom of their heart for the rest of their life. We must think of that today. We must remember those fellow citizens of ours who lie in a foreign land because they performed their duty.
March 12, 1974

We must remember those veterans who came back after carrying out their duties, crippled or disabled, and who defend upon help. We must not forget our responsibilities to those veterans who have fought for our freedom to govern and build a proud, prosperous and peace-loving Canada where Canadians can hopefully live in a climate of unity.
However, Mr. Speaker, it is more than a spirit of remembrance or a feeling of gratitude which compels me to take part in this debate. It is also a sense of justice towards our veterans who are entitled to proper living conditions and accommodations and, like any other Canadian, to the benefits provided for them in the legislation.
I am aware that the department concerned tried to explain why such a large number of veterans did not ask for these benefits, indicating that they had merely asked for eligibility certificate before October 1968, in case they should want to apply for a loan later.
Mr. Speaker, there may very well be some cases of that type but judging by the number of letters and complaints addressed to us, and I know that all members could say the same, the Veterans Land Act is still behind the times and not in keeping with the present conditions, in spite of numerous amendments made over the years.
Let us go quickly into the matter a little deeper without any claim to expertise on my part for the reasons that 1 gave from the outset. For instance, under the provisions of Part II of the Veterans Land Act, veterans may borrow up to $18,000.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that it is impossible to build a house for $18,000. One can hardly have a basement built for this amount. If the act had been amended so as to keep up with inflationary costs, thousands of veterans would be now taking advantage of their rights.
But there is an even more serious limitation and it is that related to the lot, namely the requirement for half an acre. In some cases, this figure can be reduced by 20 per cent. As everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, when planning to build a house-veterans are not alone in this situation; it is the same for all Canadians-the price of lots is so high today that it is impossible for a man to provide a house for his family.
In this area, the government has unfortunately been unable to adjust to the situation, and this at the expense of veterans. As concerns the deadline of October 1, 1968, for housing, it is difficult for me to understand the uncompromising attitude of the department in stating that every veteran had the opportunity to apply before that date. The minister is well aware that many veterans did not know about the deadline for reasons beyond their control and now have their rights denied under this charge. This is true even though the minister pretends that everyone was aware of the situation. If there ever was a time when it became imperative to put off the deadline for housing entitlement, it is right now when the housing shortage has never been so critical in Canada. Despite all its improvements the National Housing Act today cannot meet the needs of low-income people. Under the Veterans Land Act we are in a position to cope with the needs of thousands of Canadian veterans to whom the government has made a pledge years ago when the prime minister of the day
Veterans Land Act Extension
stated in 1917-a long time ago, Mr. Speaker-that no Canadian would ever say that the government was not honouring its obligation towards the veterans who had served their country.
Today, we may wonder whether the government is not repudiating the undertaking pledged in 1917? Is it being ignored? If they want to, the government can remove the deadline, for there are still a few days left until March 31.
In the light of all the speeches delivered in this House and the fact that hon. members have expressed their unanimous wish that it be done, the government would be justified in removing this deadline by means of a piece of legislation that could be introduced within a few days. The loan ceiling could be raised and the requirements relating to land could be watered down. The government could also remove all restrictions with regard to deadlines.
I am sure this position is appreciated by the minister for whom we have the greatest respect since we consider him as one of our great heroes, one of the most distinguished citizens of Canada. I am sure he will understand why we so earnestly want valiant veterans like him to be able today to count on the generosity and the sense of justice of the government toward them.
Mr. Speaker, mine is a very modest voice you have just heard. I trust the minister will hear our plea, and the government act towards the veterans as they did for the government, in a spirit of utmost generosity.

constitute a new parliament. What are the terms of the motion which would bring all this about? They are that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) ought to give consideration to extending the March 31 deadline.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext: For that reason, motions under Standing Order 43 are usually turned down by this side of the House. It is only the most exceptional motion which receives unanimous consent.
