subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for your ruling. It is true that we sit in this chamber as elected members of the House without regard for our personal backgrounds, our race, religion, creed, colour or otherwise. We are all equal members of the House and entitled to comment. I have specifically tried to set out the fact that I recognize that a debt of gratitude is due those who did don uniform-I am one of those who did not-for enabling us to raise our families in peace in this country through the service they rendered.
The nature of the legislation relating to the Department of Veterans Affairs, and specifically the Veterans Land Act, the re-establishment program, the program of educational credits extended to veterans and so on, is well known and understood, I believe, by all Canadians. When men are in the trenches we cannot compensate them with dollars and cents or with paying them an hourly wage, so the least we can do for them is to offer them some programs when they come home that will enable them to become re-established in society. Many thousands of veterans took advantage of the re-establishment programs, the educational retraining program and many other programs. In addition, they also took advantage of the benefits conferred under the Veterans Land Act, which recognized that we owed it to the veterans, as a prior right, to assist them with our tax dollars to establish a homestead.
Even the veterans pensions are based on a different premise from other pension legislation. Veterans pensions are quite different from any other kind of social welfare legislation that we have, and are in repayment of a debt of gratitude that we can never adequately repay. I think the nature and background of that legislation is very well and very widely understood. Bearing that in mind, I think we must accept the fact that the intent of the legislation which in 1968 put a deadline on the Veterans Land Act, legislation which was fully debated in this House at the time, was legislation that was also well understood. Some 25 years had elapsed since the end of the war, and most of the veterans who were to take advantage of the legislation had probably opted for it by that time. It seemed that in the interests of fiscal orderliness, to say the least, the time

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
had come when we should look to a date when the books could be closed.
As I say, this proposal was put forward in the House in 1968 and was widely debated. There was no opposition in principle at that time to the concept that the books should be brought to a close in a reasonable and orderly way so that the country could understand just what the outstanding obligation was, and what were its dimensions. Thus, the program was entered into and veterans were invited to enrol and to qualify themselves for a certificate entitling them to any benefits that were outstanding. The program was well advertised and information about it was widely distributed in the press and through the radio. There was a high level of understanding throughout the country in 1968 of this deadline date. Any veterans organization today would be able to verify that. The veterans were made very well aware of the importance of that qualifying date, and it was advertised far enough in advance. Again, I suggest that the spirit of that legislation was not challenged.
What then is the nature of the problem today? The nature of the problem is that in spite of understanding the nature of veterans benefit legislation and recognizing its merits, and also recognizing the wisdom of endeavouring at one point in our history to close the books on the benefits to World War II veterans, we have arrived at a stage today where, perhaps in isolated instances, there may be hardships to veterans. I speak with some personal knowledge of that because I can tell you there are a number of veterans in Sudbury, whom I represent, who found themselves in 1968 living in company houses owned by the International Nickel Company or Falconbridge Nickel Mines. They knew that as long as they worked for these companies they could continue to rent these houses at very reasonable rates, but never for one moment did they visualize that these houses would be offered to them for sale or, if the houses were offered for sale, that the Veterans Land Act would be of any benefit to them. Perhaps this was because the houses are very small on very small lots and would never have qualified under the program in any case.
However, both situations have changed. Therefore, there are a number of veterans about whom I have been making representations to the minister, and about whom I intend to continue to make representations, who have found themselves in a difficult position. Knowing in 1968, and I think this is the key, that a deadline had been set beyond which the provisions of the legislation would not be applicable, they did not apply for their certificates of qualification because they could not visualize these circumstances which have changed so drastically in the intervening five years. If these veterans, some 70 or 80 of them in Sudbury, could not visualize these changed circumstances in that rather short period of time, then is it not perfectly understandable that the drafters of this legislation could not envisage these changed circumstances?
Is it not, therefore, understandable that a law which was properly conceived, debated and enacted containing a deadline which was properly advertised and under which every veteran was given a proper opportunity to qualify,

may yet, despite every precaution, cause some veterans to regret today the fact they did not apply for certificates of qualification? There are others, of course, who did apply who find themselves in a position where they cannot make application by March 31 for a specific piece of property, which is what the deadline requires.
We are dealing with a small number of people and, indeed, a different kind of situation from that of the hardship which might exist under a piece of social legislation. If there is any hardship at all to the veteran and any way to counteract it to help those veterans who served this country, by somehow extending the provisions of this act or simply through straightforward generosity under a new piece of legislation, I am sure every member on both sides of this House would want to see to it that this is done.
I know the minister, whose record of service during the war is almost legend, which I think can be challenged by no one either inside or outside this House, is one who is keenly aware of the situation. Be that as it may, the circumstances surrounding the introduction of this legislation in 1968, which imposes this March 31 deadline, made it good legislation. The reason I entered this debate was to say that if circumstances come to light which indicate that a single veteran has been aggrieved, even though that may be the result of his own actions, we have to recognize that we can never adequately repay him. If there is any way that the Cabinet can be persuaded at any time to somehow extend to that veteran some kind of a privilege, whether by new legislation or by interpretation of the old legislation, that is something we must always do.
Be that as it may, we do have to proceed in an orderly way to keep the books in respect of the extended dimensions of these applications so that we can run this department in an orderly way. I am about to conclude now, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was quite amazed when listening to the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome), who has just resumed his place, at the vehement manner in which he attacked the very straightforward and simple resolution before the House this afternoon. As I understand it, the purpose of this motion is to guarantee the rights to at least 100,000 veterans in Canada who will be denied them unless prompt and emergent action is taken to extend the deadline under the Veterans Land Act, which is to be phased out on March 31, just some two weeks away.
This motion has been put forward, as demonstrated by other speakers this afternoon, because there was a unanimous agreement in the House to a motion under Standing Order 43 that the government take action to this effect. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. March 12, 1974

Knowles) praised the official opposition for bringing this motion before the House this afternoon. Therefore, I find it incomprehensible that the hon. member for Sudbury should impute political motives.
Surely it is not playing politics to express a desire on the part of members, particularly those who are veterans, that veterans' rights should be extended as expressed by a unanimous decision last November. That was not only the will of parliament, I am sure it was and is the will of the people of Canada. I say that because during my experience in the House of Commons the veterans charter is one piece of legislation that has received unanimous support from all sides of the House. I do not think it is stretching the imagination too far to suggest that the veterans' charter is regarded almost with the same sanctity as the Magna Carta in another context.
It has been my experience with successive governments that they have not only honoured the letter of the law as it was laid down under the veterans' charter, but have gone out of their way to make certain that the charter should also embrace the spirit of the law. Therefore, it is passing strange to me that we should find it necessary as members of parliament to force this government for the first time into action in this regard.
The purpose of the motion this afternoon is to force the government into action in respect of extending this legislation. In my experience, which now covers several governments since 1951, this is the first time that pressure of this kind has been necessary to get government action. I know that hon. members will stand in their places and praise the contributions of the men who served in World War II and during the Korean conflict which has added so much to the greatness of this nation. Some government spokesmen have already indicated the improvements which have been made to the veterans charter by this present administration, but I should point out that those improvements were again made under pressure.
Hitherto governments have always automatically reviewed the veterans charter in order to bring it up to date and meet changing circumstances. I think the main point behind this motion this afternoon is to indicate to the government that we feel the time has come to make a further change in the Veterans Land Act so as to bring it into line with the drastic change which has taken place, for example, in the housing situation in this country. Who could have anticipated five years ago that the cost of housing would be such that it would be prohibitive not only for veterans but for almost every other category of Canadian to have suitable housing over their heads? This is why pressure has been brought to bear in this country and in the Parliament of Canada to get the government to recognize that this change has occurred. It would appear there is unanimous support for this motion at least on this side of the House. I am hopeful that there will be the same unanimity on the government side of the House before this debate is concluded.
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) suggested that the amendment was unnecessary because veterans are getting older. We are already age 55 and above. I was surprised that the minister in his speech in the House on
Veterans Land Act Extension
March 7 took somewhat the same line when he emphasized that the need for the rehabilitation of our veteran population has now passed. I suggest this is the sort of attitude that has downgraded the benefit of doubt clause which is one of the basic rights of veterans of Canada.
In addition to discussion on the matter of extending the VLA deadline beyond March 31 of this year from time to time we hear the suggestion mentioned in this House that there is a backlog of pension applications amounting to 9,000 or 10,000. This is because the government does not give the benefit of doubt automatically to the veteran. This benefit of doubt has been one of the major rights and privileges of the veterans of Canada.
I suggest too, that to say that the need for continuing the rehabilitation program for veterans has now passed is flying in the face of the spirit of the War Veterans Allowance Act, known as the "burnt out pension". This was not contained in the original veterans charter. It came into being because it was recognized that the veterans of Canada who had served in the front line trenches and had suffered the hardships of front-line service as a result of premature aging were suffering from disabilities which were not obvious in terms of specific injury incurred in service.
This legislation was brought in to ensure that no veteran who had served his country with distinction would be denied the sustenance of life. This is the reason Parliament enacted the War Veterans Allowance Act. I suggest the same spirit is being extended under the motion we are debating here this afternoon. I do not doubt that the minister is in support of this measure. I am waiting anxiously to hear him speak in this debate. He was half-way to his feet a short time ago. I do not know why he has hesitated to take the floor. I wish he had spoken before the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) introduced the political overtones into the debate this afternoon. I am hoping that the minister who is a distinguished veteran will speak on behalf of the government this afternoon and indicate that this also is the viewpoint of the government. This is the only interpretation we can get from the unanimous vote of last November under Standing Order 43. Obviously the minister is having difficulty persuading his colleagues on this point. There are not too many of them in the House this afternoon which indicates there is not a profound interest in that fundamental right of the veterans in this regard.
I say to the minister that when one looks at the cost of a program of this kind and places it alongside the astronomical expenditures contained in the budget of the government one sees that this is indeed a small expenditure. Why should the program be phased out now? There is a housing shortage. There is inflation and there are rising costs. Rather than phasing out this program I would suggest to the government and the minister that they should be going through the procedure that has always been the practice of government of amending the Veterans Land Act in order to bring it in line with the present economic and financial circumstances which prevail in Canada. Basic to this and because the deadline is imminent should be the renewal of the 1968 and 1974 deadlines. We might even introduce a measure, because of the present crisis in housing, to provide for the rehabilitation of existing veter-

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
ans' homes to make sure that the veterans are adequately housed in the face of exorbitantly rising costs. Obviously there should be an increased ceiling because there has been no change in that regard in almost a decade.
The regulations in respect of a lot should be made compatible with the regulations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Instead of moving in to restrict the rights of the veterans in this regard the government and the minister should be making the changes some of which I have suggested this afternoon. What is happening in respect of some 150,000 veterans who have not taken advantage of the Veterans Land Act? They are forced into panic buying under coercion as a result of the deadline. This is one of the points that is made in the letters I receive. The suggestion is made that the veterans will become involved in binding financial obligations which rather than being of assistance will result in a financial albatross around their necks because they are being panicked into making a decision because of the deadline that is being imposed. The "old sweats" are reaching retirement age. The hon. member for Labelle pointed this out. Why should they be denied the right to have a home in their declining years? This was one of the purposes of the Veterans Land Act. While they may not return to the farm and become full-time farmers or perhaps even farmers occupying a small farm holding, I am sure hon. members will agree that the need for housing has increased manifold because of the housing crisis which is all too obvious today.
One hon. member directed a question to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) concerning changes made in 1959 by another government. That was in line with the necessity to streamline the legislation because it was realized that the demand in respect of the VLA provisions concerning farming and small farm holdings was lessening as the veteran population became older. But at the time those amendments were made, it was recognized that there was a need for housing facilities and accommodation and for lots that would make it possible for the veterans to be adequately housed in their declining years. There was a unanimous vote under Standing Order 43. Parliament has expressed its will. The people of Canada will express their will in no uncertain terms on this matter unless the government is inclined to accept the motion that is before the House today.

speechtext: I would just like to ask the member a question. He is quoting letters I wrote before I made my statement in the House. I say to him: Sir, if you with your experience in the House cannot quote something better than "April fool" then I suggest you had better smarten up.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
I really appreciate the minister's point of order. Here is his letter of January 17, addressed to me:
I refer to your letter to me of December 4, 1973, in which you requested that further consideration be given to extending the March 31, 1974 deadline for veterans to apply for establishment under the Veterans Land Act.
Similar representations were made by Mr. Jack Marshall, M.P., in the House on November 6 and December 4, 1973. I assure you my reply on each occasion reflected the conclusion reached after giving careful consideration to the matter-and I believe there is little to add to my remarks reported, respectively, at pages 7605 and 8423 of Hansard.
I think it is inevitable that, with respect to any terminal date, there will always be some who will find it inconvenient or impractical. We are dealing here, however, with a land settlement program which, like the other two measures that were alternative to it, was intended to assist in the rehabilitation of veterans following the completion of wartime active service rather than on retirement from post-war occupations or careers.
By March 31 next almost thirty years will have elapsed since the end of World War II. Relating this period to the intent and purpose of the act, and having regard for the arrangements that have been in effect for a number of years to facilitate the establishment of veterans still serving in the forces, I cannot help but feel that all veterans interested in land settlement assistance have had ample time in which to apply.
I appreciate your interest in this matter and regret that I am not convinced the deadlines established by Parliament nine years ago for phasing out VLA lending operations in a reasonable manner warrant alteration today.
That was less than two months ago. I have other letters from the minister's predecessor which are to the same effect, and which indicate that there has been a hardened attitude in the department, indicating that there will not be any budging on this point.
I have heard similar undertakings regarding further consideration with respect to non-resident war veterans and the war veterans allowance. The government was going to give consideration to them, serious and favourable consideration, year after year. Where are those men today? They are in the same position they were in three and four years ago. That is how much flexibility there is with respect to this matter. It hurts me to say this.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext: You are bleeding.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
The hon. member says I am bleeding. When we are talking about veterans affairs let us consider what the veteran did. I am no professional veteran, Mr. Speaker, but some people seem to have forgotten, if they ever knew, that there is an undertaking, and it is not a terminal undertaking.
There is no terminal undertaking about the rehabilitation of a veteran, whether it be five years or ten years. The 22 year old veteran parachuter in Korea-where is he today? He still has years of service left in Canada's armed forces. Is it the thought that those men should have gotten out of the forces? My God, if those veterans of World War

II and Korea had gotten out of the armed forces we would perhaps have a bare 30,000 men today, and I am not sure that that might not meet the approval of some hon. members opposite.
The fact remains that those men have as much entitlement as I have, or had. They have as much entitlement as any other man who was qualified fully for entitlement. They did not put any terminal date on service to their country. They did not put a terminal date on their exposure to danger on behalf of their country. Why should we? Why should this be done for administrative and tidying-up reasons? We are told that this is a phasing-out program. It did not change ceilings on mortgages. We are completely unrealistic today in asking a veteran in an urban community to buy half an acre of land. What silly, damn-fool nonsense is that? Land values being what they are, most veterans cannot even begin to make the down payment on land today.
Incidentally, there are close to 100,000 men who were qualified in 1968. Their applications have to be approved or not as of March 31, 1974, and they may not qualify. There can be no mortgage disbursements beyond 1977, but there are scores and scores of veterans who will not come out of the service until 1976 or 1977. Who among us will tell a man who was 22 or 23 when he was in Korea, "I am sorry, but Canada's undertaking to you has been statute-barred. We have barred, by the statute of limitations, your entitlement which was unrestricted as declared because you served your country. We are now going to impose this statute of limitations"? All I can say to such a suggestion, Mr. Speaker, is "Shame". There is not one administrative argument that is valid, even if only a dozen men have entitlement.
I know what government administration is involved. I have been around here for a long time. But, Mr. Speaker, consider the rights of these men. Should we in the first instance have told them, "You are subject to limited gratitude, with a time expiry, and even though you have served your country with continuous service we are going to deprive you of those rights"? There is no way I can accept that and there is no way the great majority of Canadians will accept it.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was eloquent in outlining the undertaking. Other hon. members have read it into the record. The Canadian Corps, the Royal Canadian Legion, countless letters that members receive, as well as veterans who have made personal representations, all say that this deadline should be extended. I would have hoped that we could go much further. Certainly, I intend to go much further. I do not intend to desist from asking that mortgage ceilings be raised. That will not cost the government one jot or tittle. I will ask that the maximum with regard to land values be changed and that all the restrictions which apply at present be looked at, so we can give to those men who have entitlement benefits which are in proportion to those they received originally.
We know that part of the VLA was designed to provide housing for servicemen when housing was very tough to get. In many instances it was non-existent after the war.
March 12, 1974

Where is it today? As far as many of them are concerned, it is non-existent. Physically it may be there, but financially it is not. Is this to be Marie Antoinette's cake which they are to eat instead of bread? That shows, I think, what is wrong and why this program has to be updated. It may cost us a few dollars. Certainly the increase in mortgages and the restrictions with regard to the increase will need to be dealt with so that a mortgage is within reach of the veteran. The veteran is going to repay this money: it will not cost the Crown anything. There is not one iota of gain in this so far as the veteran is concerned. So why do we not go ahead and let the veteran who wants to, and who may be able to, avail himself of what is his entitlement and right?
Today there are sergeants, sergeant-majors, captains and majors who started out as troopers or aircraftsmen. Quite a few of them have worked their way up and been promoted. They have given their lives to the service of their country. Many of them saw war service which entitles them to benefits under the Veterans Land Act. Are they to be deprived merely because somebody says, "But it is 30 years since the end of the war"? What have these men been doing in the interval? Have they been on a free ride? Not very likely. And what about service wives and families who are posted every three years and live in PMQ's, or on the economy as it is euphemistically called. They have had hard, tough lives and have never been able to say, "This is my home." Now we are turning around and telling many of them, "You cannot now have a home." That is the effect of the government's action, Mr. Speaker. I hope the minister reads my speech.

Mr. Speaker, listening to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) made me wonder whether he had read with care the motion put forward earlier today and debated so cogently by spokesmen of his party. The motion reads:
This House regrets that the government has not extended the March 31, 1974, deadline under the Veterans Land Act and calls upon the government to consider taking immediate steps to extend this deadline.
The minister-I think this must be said in all candour- has changed his mind. On Thursday in this House, when speaking in the throne speech debate, he indicated that
Veterans Land Act Extension
having given the matter some consideration he had reached the conclusion that the course of action requested by members of all parties should not be followed. I stress that members of all parties put forward these views, because some partisan speeches have just been made. I am thinking of the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) and the hon. member for Edmonton West, who indulged in what I regard under the circumstances as unnecessary, partisan rhetoric.
In any case, last week the minister concluded that he could not grant the extension which many members in all parties desired. He has come forward today and has candidly said he has listened to the voices from both sides of the House who have urged that the government reconsider its position. He made an unequivocal commitment today that the government will make such a reconsideration. One of the fundamental principles of parliamentary democracy is to be able to achieve the kind of situation we have achieved today, namely, if the members of the House of Commons exercise through their voting power, behind which lies reason, a change or shift in government direction, that is what parliamentary democracy is supposed to be all about.
I say quite frankly that my party has been able to support the present government on a number of specific decisions precisely because they have been prepared to move from one position one day to another position some time later.

Some members of my party are in veterans' organizations; some are not. Basically, that is irrelevant. The important question is whether we have a commitment to do justice to the men and women who served in our armed services. Many members of my party, as well as members of other parties, have made representations to the minister to not only extend the Veterans Land Act for a limited period of time but to extend it indefinitely. I will speak very briefly on that subject. What was good for men and women who risked their lives in battle in order to preserve the integrity of our nation should be offered to them for the rest of their lives. They should receive the benefits provided by this legislation. There is no principle for setting a terminal date on this legislation.

If it was deserved for serving in action or for risking their lives-if indeed it was given for that reason-it is not something the government of Canada should withdraw after so many years. Indeed, it is something that should remain with the veterans all their lives.
My second point is that there is need for improvement in the legislation. After the minister has further considered this matter I urge there will be a positive decision. I hope the legislation will not simply be extended in its present form but will be improved along the lines suggested by the Canadian Corps Association, the Legion, a number of other bodies and members of this House.
I wish to make a suggestion that has not yet been made in this debate. Any provision in the act for World War II veterans should apply to members of peacekeeping forces in the Middle East or Cyprus. In fact, it should apply to all members of the Canadian armed services in the recent past or indefinite future as long as they are prepared to risk their lives for the preservation of our country or for what it stands.
In conclusion, I welcome the minister's commitment to the House that the cabinet will give serious consideration to this extension. I hope the consideration will take place soon, that the decision reached will be a positive one and that the veterans of this country will get their just dues.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to participate in this debate and to speak after the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) whom I understood to say-and he can correct me if I am wrong-that he will oppose this motion. I take it from his statement that he will vote against the motion. If I am wrong in that assumption, he can correct me. I am glad that he is satisfied with what the minister said. In his satisfaction he showed that easy acceptance of government positions which this party has not been prepared to accept from time to time. I accept the minister personally. From reading between the lines of what he has said here and elsewhere, I believe he would genuinely like to be able to accept our motion.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) would genuinely like to be able to come into this House and say that his cabinet colleagues have authorized him to categorically indicate they will in fact bring forward a bill to remove the repugnant section in the act and the deadline. However, he has not been able to do that. He has not given any unequivocal, categorical assurance, although he easily satisfied my friend from Oshawa-Whitby. I think the record will bear that out.
What is this motion? It is not couched in the loudly condemnatory terms it would have been possible for us to use. It is not, as suggested by the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome), a motion dealing with the political aspects of this very serious problem. It was said by our spokesman in this House today, as we said earlier, that we regret the government has not taken the action urged upon them by this party and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to remove this deadline. That is the position we take. We said, "Do it." We regret they have not done it.

This is probably the last opportunity that will be available to extend this deadline for the benefit of the veterans of Canada. What is there political in that? If we did not make a motion of this kind we would be derelict in our duty, because that is why we are here. I am a veteran. I have no conflict of interest because I did not qualify prior to 1968, and I have no intention of doing so. However, as a veteran I understand the feelings of other veterans.
Having said that about the motion, what has been the situation? Various motions have been put forward by my hon. friend from Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) and others. On November 9, 1973, one of my hon. friends put forward a motion as the latest of a series of attempts to focus attention upon this situation. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also sought to persuade the government to act, and the House unanimously accepted the motion. That was as far as we could go on that occasion.
My hon. friend from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) produced a letter dated January 17 of this year in which the minister indicated he was unable to accede to the request contained in that motion unanimously approved by the House. On January 11, just before the recess, the minister said he would review the position, but obviously between January 11 and January 17 the minister had taken an irrevocable decision.
If anything more was needed to convince us that this was the position of the government, a position which the minister was unfortunately compelled to put forward, I would refer to the minister's speech of March 7. I was not in the House at the t,me he made it, but I read that speech with interest. The minister built it up in careful, logical steps, reason by reason. He ended by saying he was convinced he could not accede to the request made by veterans organizations and by this House to extend the deadline. That is a clear and final expression of the minister's position. How else, then, could we act than by bringing forward the motion we have put down today, couched in terms which I consider to be mild and temperate?
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says he appreciates the view taken in the motion and would like very much to support it. Obviously, he will not do so. I refer to this matter because on May 4, 1970, the hon. member moved a motion calling upon the government "to give consideration to an immediate and substantial increase in the basic amount of the old age security pension and of veterans' pensions and allowances, and this House also urges that still further steps be taken to improve the quality of life of all our older and retired people". A procedural argument arose. I am sure that Your Honour, with the advice of your assistants, with the careful attention to detail which you always pay, has examined this matter and is not unfamiliar with the relevant citations. In the course of that debate the hon. member said:
1 quite deliberately avoided using the words "this House condemns the government" for such and such a thing because I know that there have been over the years a number of non-confidence motions, particularly in the days when there were supply motions which the opposition sought to amend, which expressed views which the government was prepared to accept; and when the government accepted those views,
March 12, 1974

saying it had no objection to the motion that had been presented, the non-confidence motion lost its non-confidence character.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was aware of this motion, aware of its significance, and in the circumstances under which this motion was drafted we did have that consideration, as well as other considerations, in mind. Now, if the minister has the authority to take a decision to abolish this deadline, let him stand up and vote for the motion; let him persuade his colleagues to vote for the motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the clock interrupted me at six o'clock I was engaged in the very fascinating pastime of inquiring why hon. friends to my left were so easily satisfied with the statement made by the minister today. Let me go into it a little more fully. What did the minister say? He said that the government would consider the possibility of extending the March 31 deadline. That is not good enough for us, Mr. Speaker. It is not good enough
Veterans Land Act Extension
for me and it is not good enough for the veterans of Canada.
The minister also said: "I am quite prepared to take another look at this whole question in the light of the pleas made today, after looking at all the evidence". That is not good enough for me either, Mr. Speaker. Also, it is not good enough for my party or for the veterans of Canada, even though it may be good enough for hon. friends to my left, who since this parliament started have parked their once great principles outside their offices and, politically speaking, have indulged in the business of political expediency ad nauseam. It may be good enough for them, but it is not good enough for us.
What else did the minister say? I think this was his concluding sentence, and it is what we must take to be the limits of his undertaking: "I will be happy to consider the whole matter again and to make a recommendation to the government". What kind of recommendation, Mr. Speaker? What is the minister going to do?
The motion we have put before the House today, couched in the words it is, is not the kind of motion that perhaps we would have liked to move. There are limitations of wording. But when you put together what we have said in our motion, we are saying that we regret the government has not indicated that it is prepared to extend the deadline and we want the government to take immediate steps to extend it-not tomorrow or the day after, but immediately. This means but one thing. It means that the minister, or if not this minister some other responsible minister, must give us an undertaking today that legislation will be brought forward to deal with the matter.
This undertaking must be given unequivocally and categorically. Legislation must be introduced by the government. I cannot do it as a private member and neither can the members of my party. Only a member of the cabinet can introduce legislation to extend the deadline, and we want the government to give an undertaking to this effect. If we do not get it, we are not satisfied.
The minister's remarks today have to be read in light of what he said just five days ago. When he spoke five days ago he was speaking calmly, with a prepared speech, following meditation and consideration on this issue that had extended over a period of months. He was not at that time under the pressure he is today, and neither was the government. What the minister said last Thursday was the careful, reasoned, calculated statement of a man representing the government. Let me refer to just one passage in the minister's statement of March 7 which appears at pages 304 and 305 of Hansard:
Almost nine years have elapsed since that deadline was established. The terminal date has been well publicized. I am of the opinion, therefore, that veterans sincerely interested in obtaining VLA benefits for the purposes contemplated by the act have had ample time in which to do so. Virtually every veteran who obtained a VLA certificate of qualification by the deadline of October 31, 1968, had already utilized the benefits alternative to those of the Veterans Land Act.
Finally the minister said:
On January 11 last, as reported at page 9182 of Hansard, I stated that if I had sufficient information to make me think the deadline date should be changed I would so recommend to the government. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I have carefully considered all relevant representations and data, including that determined by the Royal Canadian Legion in the survey it conducted last December. I am

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
unable to conclude that such a recommendation would be warranted or appropriate.
That is the cold, calculated, careful and deliberate statement of the spokesman for the government, stacked up against those weaseling words that the minister used today. I apologize for using those words about the minister because I know if he had the opportunity on his own he would not, on behalf of the government, had used the weaseling, limiting words that were used today and which can give no hope to this House or to the veterans of Canada that this deadline will be extended.
We cannot accept that, and we must press ahead with a vote on this motion unless the government indicates it intends to do something about this matter. I do not think it will, because the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) insisted on writing those words for the minister after the intercourse-I use that word in the best sense-between the two sides. There was a heavy movement which took place between the government and the NDP. Both sides knew what was going to be said, and those words were used to take my friends to the left off the hook. They think they are off the hook, but when this is all over they will be hanging suspended for all the world to see.
If there is any sense of political morality and decency left in this House, somebody on the government side will stand up before this debate is ended and give a clear, categorical assurance to the people of Canada that legislation will be introduced to extend this deadline. That is all that needs to be done, and that will be accepted. If the government will not do that, then I issue the challenge to my friends who sit over there so complacently to vote with us and force the government to accept this motion. Apparently they have no regard at all for the veterans. Perhaps I should clarify that by saying they have no regard for our veterans unless they indicate before this debate ends that they are prepared to vote with us to compel the government to accept the motion.
There are limits to what private members or the opposition can do. Day after day, session after session the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe and other members of this party who have been our spokesmen for veterans affairs, as well as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and members of the Creditiste party, have brought forward motions similar and akin to this one asking that something be done. This was not only done by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, although he has been assiduous in this matter, but by other members. However, the government has steadfastly rejected our motions and refused to give us this right, so we had no alternative but to bring forward our motion couched in these terms to find out precisely what the government is going to do. At a quarter to ten this House, its members, the people of Canada and especially the veterans will know where the government and the NDP stand on this issue.

March 12, 1974

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the entire debate this afternoon on what we put forward as a very serious matter affecting a great many veterans in this country. We heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) speak in favour of the veterans and this motion which he has moved many times before, and just now we heard the speech of the hon. member for York South (Mr. 
Lewis). Instead of taking the political course of criticizing the Conservative Party, the hon. member for York South should have asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) to give us a commitment that he would introduce an amendment to extend the deadline of this legislation.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs has made no commitment. Last Thursday, as mentioned by the hon. member for York South, the Minister of Veterans Affairs said emphatically-and it has been mentioned many times today in the House-that there would be no extension. Yet the hon. member for York South stands in his place and tries to criticize the Conservative Party. If he is sincere in his allegations, why did he not bring in an amendment to correct our motion which he says is not right? No, he just wants to play politics and keep the government in power. This matter is serious. I would call the performance we have seen "courtroom politics." I know there have been agreements and that bargains have been made, and that is why we heard the speech just made by the leader of the NDP.
Many things have concerned me for a good many years with respect to veterans who have applied for benefits under the Veterans Land Act. These veterans are probably working in the cities and in large metropolitan centres. Under the rules and regulations of the Veterans Land Act they have found it impossible to buy a house or to find a location of their choice on which to build a house, not through any fault of their own but because they are making their livelihood in the large cities of Canada. But today many of our veterans have reached the age when they can retire. I have letters here telling me that some of them have picked out locations in which to build a house in smaller communities. But what happens? One of these letters reads as follows:
I am writing you as our duly elected member of the federal government to find your views on the possibility of an extension of time from the deadline of March 31, 1974, to extend the Veterans Land Act closing date. Many veterans of the war have, for a variety of reasons, to this date not taken advantage of this form of gratuity for their service. In my own case I have not as yet taken this up. Now I wish to do this.
I have my letter of qualification from the DVA but as this must be exercised by March 31, 1974, this leaves me with a problem. I have no doubt there will be many veterans in a similar position. With the escalation of real estate prices it is almost impossible to acquire the added moneys beyond the maximum $18,000.
This veteran says in closing:
I would appreciate hearing your views and intentions in this matter. I do not know if the closure or extension would require an act of parliament or would, like the old soldier, just quietly pass away-
This is something that is happening to far too many of our veterans today: we are forgetting about them and they are expected to just pass away. I have another letter from a chap who applied. He is qualified and has submitted the deed to VLA, but he cannot build the house in the very nice location of his choice because at present there are no sewers servicing the property. However, within two years there will be such services to this area. This is what we are denying our veterans by closing out on March 31, and that is why I beg the minister, who is a sane and reasonable man, to extend this deadline.
March 12, 1974

If the minister had today given the House his word that the deadline would be extended, not that he would take the matter up, I am sure a different course would have been taken in the House today. This is a serious matter. My friends to the left are trying to make us believe that we are just playing politics. That is not so. With very few days left, the veterans are duly concerned. And why should they not be concerned? For far too long we have neglected our veterans who have offered their lives so that we may have the freedom which we enjoy in this great country of ours. They did not ask us, "What will you give us when we join?" They did not ask us, "What have you to offer us?" They served hoping that they would come back with their lives. They were ready to lay down their lives in order to give us a better way of life in a free world.
All they asked was to be fortunate enough to come back; and they had faith in us to grant them some consideration for their services. They did not barter with us. They went, they offered their services and some of them lost their lives. The least we can do is to give them some consideration in return. I want to emphasize again that many thousands of veterans are planning their retirement and are begging for an extension of the Veterans Land Act. I hope an extension will come about.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to be asked to speak again on a motion put forward by the able veterans affairs critic of the official opposition, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). I spoke on a motion moved by the hon. member on May 18 of last year. That was also a motion to urge this House to meet a solemn obligation to those of our citizens who fought in Canada's wars.
I doubt that there is a member of this House who does not go back to his riding from time to time and tell veterans groups that their parliament recognizes their sacrifices and that we accept the obligation and responsibility to them that has been passed down to us by previous parliaments. Yet we seem to be continually debating in this House whether we will in fact honour the pledges that have been passed to us and which we ourselves have made.
It seems to me at times that this government approaches legislation dealing with veterans as though it were something to be got over with as quickly as possible and at the least cost to the public treasury as possible. I have heard statisticians remark that veterans of World War I will all be dead by such and such a time, and that veterans of other wars will all be dead by a certain time. Then they go about working out cost estimates of the various programs that we have set up to look after veterans. These are not statistics or mortality tables with which we are dealing. These are brave men and women who answered the call when we were being pushed to the wall. These are people, Canadians, human beings. These are people who hate war because they know how horrible war is. These are people who knew when they left home that they might never return. It sometimes appears to me there are people who wish they could just forget that these people did come back; who wish we could just forget about them until we need them again. That is the feeling I get when I hear members of parliament debating dollars and cents when they should be debating how soon they can pass a bill to
Veterans Land Act Extension
erase some of the wrongs we have committed against veterans and their families through our omissions and our procrastinations.
Statistics and actuarial tables aside, we are thinking and talking about veterans who are alive, veterans who have aspirations and problems and dreams that are no different from those of other people. Those of past generations who gave their lives in our wars are honoured in many ways- with statues, parks, buildings, scholarships, and on memorial days. This is fitting, and in this respect I believe we are living up to our solemn responsibilities. I believe that the vast majority of people honestly and sincerely acknowledge their debt to those who died in order that we might live. However, we owe the same debt of gratitude and thanks to the living veterans and the monuments we erect to those veterans must be living monuments. The Veterans Land Act is just such a living monument and it must be kept alive.
There was no intention, on the part of the parliament that passed the act back in 1942 that it should be terminated before the end of its useful life. It was passed as veterans' legislation and it has the same validity and purpose today as it had in the year it was enacted. No one would suggest that we should phase out veterans pensions, veterans hospitals-at least I hope not-or war veterans allowance simply because some statistician can produce a time when he says all veterans will have passed from the scene. Why, then, should anyone single out the VLA and suggest that it should be given an expiry date?
A previous parliament passed an act that would extend to veterans the right to borrow money from their government to purchase land and a home. They were not told that they had to sit down, there and then, and decide where they would like to build a home or when they would be able to start. A later parliament, or perhaps I should say a later government, decided that this right granted to veterans must have some strings attached to it. Veterans were told to make up their minds by a certain date, or forget it. We have been told during the past few days, and in fact we were told in this House and in committee meetings last year, that the veterans had been given ample warning that VLA was going to be terminated and that any veterans who wanted to qualify had sufficient time to get in under the wire.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, it has been ably stated by many of my colleagues, on all sides of the House, that there is no compelling reason why an expiry date should have been imposed and no good reason why that expiry date should be allowed to stand. It is for us today in this House to decide whether or not that expiry date should be expunged from the record. We are not bound by any past government or any past parliament in this matter. Experience has shown us that the expiry date is unpopular with those for whom VLA was established, and if it is unpopular with the veterans then we must reinstate this very important legislation.
I could talk at length about the positions that have been taken by my colleagues in today's debate. But, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer in particular to some remarks made by the very able veterans affairs critic for the New

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
Democratic Party, himself a veteran, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). During the debate of last May on a motion moved by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, the hon. member for Timiskaming proposed a solution that was excellent at that time, and I believe it would be as acceptable today not only to his party but to mine as well.
The hon. member for Timiskaming outlined a three-part proposal that would extend the Veterans Land Act provisions and would also raise the ceiling on loans from $18,000 to $25,000. The increase in loan ceiling would erase part of the effect of inflation on land prices and in my opinion is an excellent proposal. On the hon. member's first point I quote from Hansard for May 18, 1973:
First, we will have to convince the minister and his officials that it is necessary to wipe out the qualifying date, at least with regard to smallholdings.
The "we" to whom he referred were the members of this House. The second point dealt with the raising of the loan ceiling, while his third point dealt with the alleged problem of administering the smallholdings provisions in the Veterans Land Act. He proposed that if this indeed was a problem for the Department of Veterans Affairs, then it could and should be turned over to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for administration.
While I accept the hon. member's proposals as going a long way toward solving this problem, if it is a problem, I cannot accept the argument that the high cost of administering the program is a valid excuse for allowing the government to squirm out of the responsibility for continuing VLA beyond the present expiry date. Every program that we have in operation at the present time has its own administrative problems and administrative costs. But the programs go on and we continue to establish new ones.
The reasons for continuing the VLA program are obvious, and there are many of them. First of all, as I and many of my colleagues have said, the VLA program was designed for veterans, and as long as there are veterans who want to take advantage of the program then the Veterans Land Act should be available to them.
Another good reason is that before the arbitrary deadline to qualify for a VLA entitlement certificate passed on October 31, 1968, 150,000 veterans had been issued certificates. Of that number only about 25,000 have actually received the benefit of the program. This means that 125,000 certificate holders have yet to decide where they want to build and when they would like to start. Obviously, there are some certificate holders who will not take advantage of the program no matter how long they have to make up their minds. I think the minister also alluded to this fact. And it is likely that quite a number of those to whom certificates were issued are not living today. However, Mr. Speaker, this is not a criterion for deciding whether to retain the VLA program or to allow it to die 20 days from now. As long as there are any veterans at all who have not taken advantage of the program, it must be retained for them.
In addition to the veterans of past wars who returned to civilian life there are many, perhaps several hundred, who are still serving in the armed forces. Right now they must be wondering if we are really going to extend something to them with one hand and take it away from them with

the other. Some of these people will not be out of the forces for another five or six years. They may be presently serving in Egypt, Cyprus or Germany. How can they be expected to know at this point where they will decide to settle a few years from now or when they will be ready to start building?
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) made some interesting remarks during the debate this afternoon. I would like to refer to two of them. First of all he said that the government of Canada in 1942 was forced to provide some sort of incentive to Canadians to volunteer for service, and that one of the incentives was the Veterans Land Act. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, then I cannot think of a more solemn pledge for a parliament to pass along to all succeeding parliaments. If we are to take the hon. member's remarks on faith, then the government of that time said that anyone who would volunteer to risk life and limb in the service of his or her country would be rewarded by, among other things, the right to settle or resettle under the provisions of the Veterans Land Act. Could the hon. member deny that this is a pledge that has not been completely fulfilled? And could the hon. member deny that this pledge has been passed to us and must be passed along to succeeding parliaments so long as there is one living veteran?
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I must accept the version which says Canada was able to maintain the largest volunteer force overseas of any country engaged in World War II and that it was able to do this without incentives and without conscription. Further, the hon. member for Labelle suggested that those veterans who have already taken advantage of VLA could be angered by any move on our part to increase the ceiling on loans from $18,000 to $25,000. I doubt that, for a couple of reasons. In the first place, the original ceiling was $12,000 and it was raised to $18,000 for the same reason we are proposing to raise it to $25,000.
Further, the homes that were built ten years ago at a cost of $18,000 are now worth $36,000 or more, and there is no way in which those who build now are going to realize such a dramatic gain in equity over that period. Another reason is that the veterans organizations themselves are pushing hardest for the extension of VLA and for the increase in loan ceiling. Many of those who are pressing the issue are veterans who have not taken advantage of VLA.
I would like to end my remarks by referring to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). I said in my speech in May, 1973, that the Minister of Veterans Affairs was admirably suited, by experience and temperament, to the task he has undertaken. He has shown compassion and understanding as well as objectivity in his approach to veterans problems. However, Mr. Speaker, I have detected a change in the minister during the past few months.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
It is not a change for the better, in my opinion. It is a change I have detected especially since last month. In February the minister gave
March 12, 1974

every indication that he viewed with some favour the representations of veterans groups urging the extension of the Veterans Land Act. The minister has since been accused of raising false hopes in the minds of veterans. I cannot believe, or at least I do not want to believe that the minister would build up the hopes of veterans groups on a premise that he knew to be false.
Did the minister really believe that his cabinet colleagues would support him in a bid to extend or remove the deadline on VLA applications? I want to believe he was sincere, but today he made some statements which seem puzzling. For instance, the minister said he would be prepared to take another look at the Veterans Land Act question. He would take another look at what? That he never intended to push for extension? Also, he said he would be happy to reconsider; that is, to reconsider if he considers it to be warranted. Again, he poses the question as to what would or might be warranted. Did he mean the extension of the deadline, or did he mean the Veterans Land Act itself? After all, Mr. Speaker, the Veterans Land Act is the expression of the will of parliament-of several parliaments. I hope the minister does not mean that he will consider at some later date whether he feels the Veterans Land Act to be warranted. I cannot help feeling that the Canadian people will have the last word on that matter.
By not extending the deadline of the Veterans Land Act the Liberal government appears to have conspired to get us to use up one of our opposition days, Mr. Speaker.

I cannot think of a better way to use up an opposition day than drawing attention to Canada's veterans and the need to preserve and update vital veterans programs. We make no apology for that, Mr. Speaker. Regardless of what the leader of the NDP says, this has not been a partisan debate.
In conclusion I want to take members back to a Remembrance Day ceremony of past years and to a short poem recited by a legionnaire which goes like this:
No doubt he cherished his life,
Not unlike you and I,
But if we take for granted The reason that he died,
We don't deserve our freedom,
Because we've never learned It was our peace and liberty,
These brave soldiers earned
My hon. friends, if we fail to build a better world for our returning veterans, the hero in that poem died in vain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at first blush the motion before the House today might appear to be a routine opposition day motion, as it calls on the government to consider taking immediate steps to extend
Veterans Land Act Extension
the deadline for the phasing out of the Veterans Land Act beyond March 31 this year. On looking more closely we find that it is a motion of non-confidence against the government, moved under section 58(4) (a) of our rules of procedure. So it is a motion on which the House will divide, something which is most unusual. Why do I say that? In the six years I have been a member of parliament, this is the first time the House has divided on party lines on a matter relating to veterans who served this country so gallantly in war and so capably in the building of the country since the war.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), when he spoke, almost seemed to excuse himself and his party as, half humorously, he called on members on our side of the House to support a motion which he knows is a motion of non-confidence. I suggest that if any member on this side wanted to join the PC party, he would do it directly and not by supporting a "bassackwards" motion like the one now before the House. The theory of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Beattie) was interesting. He suggested that there was a government conspiracy for the government to use up or waste an opposition day. That is a strange theory, as the opposition party chose and moved the motion which is now before us.
I served on the veterans affairs committee during sessions of the last parliament and from time to time in the first session of the present parliament. I can say sincerely that it has been a non-partisan committee which has rarely divided. Usually, all members worked together and discussed a matter until consensus was arrived at. That is why I feel so uncomfortable about this debate, because for the first time in several years we are seeing a partisan approach to the problems of veterans.
There are fewer veterans who are members of the House now as compared with the last Parliament when I believe about 25 per cent of our members were veterans. Of course, the percentage of veteran members at present is considerably lower than it was in the first parliament after 1945. Nevertheless, the veterans affairs committee of the twenty-eighth parliament was perhaps one of the busiest committees of the House of Commons. Naturally, all committees worked more because the rules were changed and the estimates of various departments were considered in committee and not in committee of the whole. Even so, the veterans affairs committee did a tremendous job in that parliament. It studied the Woods committee report and made recommendations to the government which resulted in Bill C-203 coming forward. It was the most complete overhaul of pension legislation affecting veterans to be introduced in the last 50 years.
There was a tremendous spirit of co-operation among the parties and veterans associations. That, essentially, was the spirit in which the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs worked, the committee in which the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) has been a most active member. As I said, the committee worked in a non-partisan way. Its efforts were bent to providing better pensions, better health services, better welfare services and more special assistance to veterans, rather than to partisan activity.
The bill I have mentioned was a milestone in pension legislation. It provided for the Pension Review Board to be
446

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
separate and independent from the Canadian Pension Commission, for the establishment of the independent bureau of pension advocates, for the exceptional incapacity allowance, for a stronger benefit of the doubt clause and for special benefits for Hong Kong prisoners of war.
The idea of extending the VLA deadline is not new. It was extended in 1959 to 1962, in 1962 it was extended to 1968 and in 1965 it was extended from 1968 to 1974. This afternoon the minister said he would give serious consideration to extending this deadline beyond the March 31 limit established back in 1965. We are proud of our Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
We are proud of his career in wartime; we are proud of his career as a farmer in his native province of Prince Edward Island; we are proud of his record as minister of agriculture in that province and the work he has done in this parliament.
A year ago the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs recommended that benefits to veterans on a 100 per cent incapacity allowance be increased by relating them to the standard of living which would be directly related to the minimum federal civil service wages. Some members considered it would be very difficult for the minister to persuade his cabinet colleagues to adopt this principle which had first been proposed in 1918 or 1919. Veterans organizations had made representations on this for many years. It was the present Minister of Veterans Affairs who was able to bring forward this legislation last spring and have it adopted in order that the veterans of this country would receive a pension related to the minimum wage rates of the federal civil service.
We are proud of the way the minister has kept the budget of the Department of Veterans Affairs in line with what these men and women require. I note that in 1972 the departmental budget was $432 million. In his speech today the minister announced that in the 1974-75 estimates it will be $597 million, an increase of $165 million for the some 200,000 in this country who receive some level of pension benefits.
Unlike the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who spoke this afternoon suggesting they were not able to accept the assurances of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, I am willing to accept the word of the minister that he intends to review this matter and place recommendations before cabinet. Taking into account the minister's distinguished war record, I am sure most members of this House are willing to accept the minister's word.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it an honour to take part in this debate and to endorse the motion put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). I would in fact go further and offer him my congratulations and the thanks of many, many people in the constituency I represent for having brought this urgent and important matter before the House of Commons today.

I was equally impressed with the remarks of the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the eloquent and passionate manner in which he pleaded with the minister and all in this House to agree to an extension of the deadline of March 31, 1974, when the government proposes to phase out the Veterans Land Act. These speeches dealt with the issue in a non-partisan and compassionate way; compassionate because at stake are the future plans of many thousands of Canadians who served in World War II and the Korean war.
The government's proposal to phase out the Veterans Land Act at the end of this month has met with a strong variety of responses from members on all sides of the House-from strong objection to at least serious reservation. Regardless of some of the heated remarks made earlier today, I hope that when this motion is voted on we will be united as a parliament in seeing that humane treatment is accorded to that large body of men and women throughout this country who genuinely deserve our consideration.
The constituency of Kingston and the Islands has a long history of military involvement. For over 300 years it has continued as a base for armed forces operations. Today its inhabitants include many who are still actively serving in the forces as well as many hundreds of former service personnel who have retired. Among the latter group are numerous individuals who have submitted applications so that they can qualify for loans under the VLA. The fact that they have not taken advantage of their applications is due largely to the inflexible terms of the act, terms which indeed prohibit them from purchasing their own homes.
The $18,000 limit for a lot and a house is a ludicrous figure in this day and age. The $18,000 would hardly pay for the lot, let alone the home, and the one-half acre stipulation has its own restrictions. For those wishing to locate on farmland in the country the acreage is inadequate. For those wishing to purchase land in a suburban area of the constituency the one-half acre lot is too large. These are factors within the Veterans Land Act that could be significantly modified if the government were to accept the motion presented by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe. Extension of the deadline should allow sufficient time for consideration to be given to modifying the act in terms of contemporary values.
For the men and women still serving in our armed forces, men and women who served throughout World War II and the Korean War, the phasing-out of the Veterans Land Act is particularly reprehensible. It is true they could have taken their discharge at the termination of hostilities; taken advantage of the benefits offered to them at that time under the Veterans Land Act and gone on to other and perhaps more lucrative careers. Instead, they chose to stay and serve, serve in our Canadian armed forces, make it a career, bring to it the high respect and renown it has maintained down through the years. The government's reward to them is to deny them the benefits they had been led to expect were theirs.
For men and women still serving in the forces and with some years still to go before retirement it is well nigh impossible to say what particular lot or piece of land they may wish to purchase. In fact, many have not yet determined where they will reside upon retirement from the
March 12, 1974

forces. How can they take advantage of the loans available under the Veterans Land Act before the March 31 deadline, when they are in no position to even consider the purchase of a lot or the construction of a home? Their present endeavours are directed to the contribution they are making in the active forces of our country, not in thinking about retirement. Of necessity, they have become used to a life of mobility and change and many of them would find it impossible at the present time to decide where they will reside when they have retired. But surely the government's contribution to their retirement should not be to refuse them the benefits that have been accruing to them, just because they chose to continue serving their country. One of my constituents has written as follows:
I have served in the armed forces continuously since World War II and can continue to serve in my present rank until February, 1976-if promoted, until February, 1978. Due to frequent service postings I have had neither the time nor the opportunity to exercise my entitlement to build under VLA. In fact, with the possibility of one or two more postings I have not even selected a possible geographic location.
It would appear that those of us who elected to continue serving are being penalized, first, by the increase in interest rates a few years ago, and, secondly, by a closure date which will prevent many of us from taking advantage of our entitlement.
It is interesting to note that he uses the word "closure". This is a word that the government certainly knows something about.
It is a well known fact that the morale of the armed forces is not at an all-time high. There have been frustrations, disappointments and setbacks for many of those who chose the military as a career. The marvel is that they maintain their present high standards despite these frustrations. But I know, having talked to many of them both in my constituency and elsewhere, that the phasing-out of the Veterans Land Act, the denial of justice to these people, would be a blow to their morale that is uncalled for, unjustified and unnecessary.
Earlier today my hon. friend from Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe said this question goes beyond the materialistic; that there is a principle involved, the principle that we should not break faith with those to whom a commitment was made in the name of the government of Canada and the people of Canada. I deplore a situation in which any of us might stand accused of having broken faith needlessly and over such a small matter when viewed in terms of dollars and cents. For the number of people who can ultimately take advantage of the VLA is not large in terms of our over-all population, and the funding required is minimal in terms of our over-all budget.
A debate such as this calls into consideration many of the old-fashioned virtues such as trust, faith, civility- virtues often overlooked in this day and age, but virtues which can and must be applied in the case of Canada's veterans if we in this House are to merit the term "responsible representatives". Every day I receive letters of appeal from those whose future security is jeopardized by the manner in which the government has vacillated in regard to this act.
Today the minister said he is prepared to consider an extension. For my part, I am willing to accept his word as given in good faith-that he and his colleagues will give
Veterans Land Act Extension
earnest consideration to the positive, humane aspects of extending the deadline while rejecting their present negative, discriminatory approach. Having given his word, having raised the expectations of thousands of veterans and servicemen, having given them cause to believe that their case is a just one and that they can hope for some action within the next 19 days, let him come forward with legislation to extend the deadline within those 19 days. Let him not dash the hopes of veterans by peremptorily announcing on March 31 that his promise to consider an extension has not led to the results they desire, that his words were hollow rhetoric.
If this is his intention, if this is the government's way of getting off what they consider to be a sticky wicket, better the minister should stand here this evening and tell the House, the veterans organizations and the nation the truth as to his intentions, for he is dealing with people who, above all else, do not deserve to be misled. I urge the minister and those associated with him to give an unequivocal guarantee to the House that the March 31 deadline will be extended.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the previous speaker, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), who told us with some pride that the constituency she has the honour to represent has a distinguished military history. If I were in her place, I would say exactly the same thing. I might remind hon. members, though, that all of us should have great pride in the constituencies we represent because I am sure that in times of trouble, in times of war, all Canadians have enlisted and done their duty for king and country.
Having said this, may I suggest the hon. lady should remember, again with pride, that a great deal has been done for veterans not only in the constituency she so proudly represents but in constituencies right across Canada, because nowhere in the world have veterans been treated so kindly as in this great country of ours. I speak not only of the present government but of previous governments. I speak as a veteran of six years' service, as one who served in all the active theatres in the last war. I listened with tears in my eyes as opposition speakers suggested that nothing had been done for the veterans of Canada. The fact is that more has been done for Canadian veterans, including the veterans of Kingston and the Islands, than anywhere else in the world, bar none.
