When we consider the motion put forward by the opposition today we should not think in terms of the Veterans Land Act alone. If the minister had not said he might change his mind, a deadline would, it is true, he applied to the legislation on March 31. We should think of other things. For example, there just happened to come into my hands tonight a number of figures as to monthly rates of disability pensions paid to veterans under the Pension Act. I do not say these veterans are getting too much, by any means. As a matter of fact, over the years, along with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and many others in this House, I have striven to secure increases for veterans because I believe pensions should increase with the cost of living. But con-

sider this. Today a married pensioner with one child receives $541 a month absolutely tax free. And it should be tax free. The fact is, he or she is getting this rate in this Canada of ours. This increase was given by this House of Commons, and all members of the House should be proud of the fact that we have looked after our veterans better than any other country in the world.
May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that our veterans also have other benefits, such as war veterans allowance for which my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre has fought so valiantly over the years, as have the rest of us though perhaps not quite so eloquently as he. Nevertheless, legislation unequalled anywhere in the world has benefited our veterans in Canada. As a matter of fact, the wealthiest country of the world, the United States, has no legislation that equals or can even be closely compared with our war veterans allowance. As I myself have said on many an occasion, only two countries of the world have a minister of veterans affairs. One of them is France. The other is not the United States, the wealthiest country in the world, or England, or Germany, or Japan; it is Canada.

speechtext:
This is why I am pleased to be a member of this House of Commons, and I say to my hon. friends in the Tory opposition that they should be proud of it too. They should be proud for three or four reasons, one of which is that the legislation that has given Canadian veterans the highest pension in the world was passed to a large extent by their own votes.
As far as I can remember, during the few years I have been here veterans pensions, legislation concerning the Veterans Land Act, and so on, have been discussed and have passed through this chamber by unanimous vote. In all sincerity I suggest that the motion put before the House today by my hon. friends on the opposition benches is, as far as I am concerned, politics at its very lowest. They are trying to take advantage of the veterans of Canada who have fought and died for this country. They are trying to overturn the government because they have been unable to do so in any other way, and they are now trying to hang this on the necks of our veterans.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
The other day I heard the remark that the bigger they are, the nicer they are. As far as this opposition motion is concerned, I say to my Conservative friends, "Sit down, Shorty". I am sure it is not one that they will be proud of in years to come.
I cannot be critical of the Veterans Land Act, because I happen to be one of those veterans who was successful in obtaining a block of land under the Veterans Land Act. Fortunately, I received my piece of land in the year 1946, at a time when many people had a similar opportunity. Many others have had this opportunity over the past 29 years and have taken advantage of it, and for that they deserve our admiration.
On the other hand, they should remember that this opportunity was given to them not just by the Liberal

Party but also by the Conservative Party who are condemning this provision today. It was also granted to them by our New Democratic friends, and indeed by our Creditiste friends. It was agreed to unanimously by this House and it is one of the pieces of legislation that I am very proud of indeed.
If I were going to be critical of the Veterans Land Act, I would suggest to my Conservative friends who have moved this motion that perhaps they should change the "V" to a "C". This legislation has proved to be a most successful housing project and has greatly assisted many veterans who live in this great country of ours. If it has been successful for our veterans, perhaps it could be successful for all Canadians. Perhaps we should change the wording of the Veterans Land Act to the "Canada land act" and give all Canadians the opportunity that our veterans have had over the years. I think this would help the housing situation in which we find ourselves today. If my Conservative friends would put forward such a suggestion, I would be the first to support it.
However, the Conservatives are hanging this motion on changing the deadline from March 31 to some time in the future. When we think that the Conservative Party is challenging Canada, that there could be an election tomorrow or even in two years as a result of this motion, then I say my Conservative friends are playing with Canadians. They are not playing with us, because we regard ourselves as at least semi-professionals; they are playing with Canadian citizens from Vancouver to St. John's, Newfoundland.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, there are other subjects that are more appropriate. As a member of the government party I can think of some myself, as a matter of fact. Quite frankly, if hon. members opposite are looking for an opposition motion, let them come and have a chat with me and I will give them one that is far better than the one they moved this afternoon.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO EXTEND DEADLINE OF VETERANS LAND ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of this motion moved by my colleague for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) because of my sincere concern for the position of many veterans in respect of the deadline, that this government insists will be kept, regarding their right to acquire a home under part
March 12, 1974

II of the Veterans Land Act, a provision that has already been fully explained in previous speeches today.
I am a little surprised at the speech just completed by the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher). I had always considered him to be a reasonably fair member. However, I think history will prove who is playing politics in this House today. I do not think anyone on this side of the House has been criticizing the legislation we have already passed for our veterans. Certainly we agree that our veterans have a lot of good legislation. What we are criticizing is the fact that veterans in Canada today are concerned about what is going to happen and they are confused by the government's inaction at the present time.
As the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe stated, this motion is being presented as a last-ditch plea to this government, in the very limited number of days left before the end of the month, to reconsider its very negative stand in regard to extending the deadline on this important provision. It is not a cheap political ploy, as some hon. members have frantically tried to make out today. To me, the main thrust of this motion originated from a commitment made many years ago by the then prime minister of Canada, Sir Robert Borden, who in a speech in 1917 had this to say:
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of your people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion. That the country will support the government to prove to the returned men its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire, and that no man, whether he goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken faith with the men who won and the men who died.
That was a pretty strong statement from the prime minister of the day, and some 50 years since that date similar statements have been uttered. However, never before, as now in 1974, due to the rapid rate of inflation as it effects our veterans of all wars, is there such a need for change in all acts referring to veterans, and there is a particular need to change this particular part of the Veterans Land Act which we are debating.
While it is true there have been many improvements over the years as conditions have changed, it is also true that there are many thousands of veterans who, possibly through their own ingenuity and good fortune, need not be concerned for the future and their own well-being. Nevertheless, thay are sincerely concerned about the well-being of their fellow comrades who are not so fortunate but who, in the minds of members of our party, still deserve full consideration. Members of this party are anxious to ensure that no veteran will be denied the right to acquire a home under part II of the Veterans Land Act because of the restrictions presently imposed, which include of course the October, 1968, deadline for certification, the March, 1974, deadline for application, the phasing-out of the act, the restricted lot requirements, land costs in urban centres and the financial ceilings which inhibit loan applications.
Like many of my colleagues, I have received numerous letters from veterans who through no fault of their own somehow missed the deadline of October, 1968, for certification. Just because of their oversight, it is difficult for me
Veterans Land Act Extension
to understand the position the department is taking in stating that everyone had an opportunity to apply before that date. Surely the minister recognizes the fact that many veterans were not knowledgeable of the deadline and are now being denied their rights under the charter.
Even though the minister has stated that we have no right to deviate from the legislation as it now stands, it has to be admitted that there have been many hundreds of amendments brought forth in the last 50 years, along with many new pieces of legislation, because of increasing costs and lot requirements as land values and availability have changed from time to time.
The veterans are not asking for the extension of just another give-away program, which is so prevalent within the government of today. They are asking for the right to continue to borrow money at a reasonable rate of interest, with the opportunity to pay it back. It has been mentioned by several previous speakers that the $18,000 ceiling should be raised, and I most heartily agree. A figure of $30,000 has been mentioned and that appears to me to be within reasonable limits, depending on just how fast the inflationary spiral we find ourselves in today keeps going up.
Another area which is closely related to the concerns expressed in this debate which I should like to refer to briefly is the right of the spouse of a veteran who qualifies under the Veterans Land Act to have the same rights and privileges as the marriage partner in respect of title to property. I have had this point brought to my attention, as I am sure have many other members. In essence, the wife of a veteran who has a VLA mortgage does not have any legal claim to the property until such time as there is an estate. In this day and age of the so-called free society, if the husband chooses to simply take off and not honour his mortgage obligations the wife could then find herself in a very financially embarrassing situation.
As a working wife and mother, such a marriage partner could have contributed as much money to the home as her husband. But even if she did not work outside the home, her contribution as a wife and mother would still be sizeable in meeting the mortgage obligations over the years. To me, this is a very important area that I feel is supplementary to this motion which is so clearly emphasized here today.
As I understand the act, any time a veteran becomes separated or divorced, the wife cannot claim any right to the property until the mortgage is paid off. But by that time the family may be grown up and the wife may not need too much help. If the husband becomes ill, mentally or otherwise, or is incompetent for any reason, the public trustee takes over the administration of the property to which the wife, as I have said before, may have contributed a sizeable effort in keeping the mortgage payments up to date.
Although departmental administrators of the legislation in most cases act in good faith, their answers to some of the questions raised by veterans and their wives do not give those Canadians the confidence I feel they deserve in order that their remaining days be as free of frustration as possible. One such departmental answer is this: The arrangement as it now stands has not created any undue hardship so long as the family relationship remains

March 12, 1974
Veterans Land Act Extension
normal, because when the veteran's debt is paid off, the title is conveyed to the veteran and upon its registration the wife's dower rights are attached. If requested, the director will convey title to a husband and wife as tenants in common, or joint tenants. If the veteran dies, the wife takes over the agreement with the director and may enjoy all the benefits that would otherwise accrue to the husband.
That is all true, but the one reference in that statement which is the key to the concern I have tried to outline is the part which says that as long as a family relationship remains normal, that is the case. As we look around today we see many family relationships that are not necessarily normal, and this is where the concern of the spouse arises. I feel it is a legitimate concern. The director will convey the title to the husband and wife as tenants in common, or joint tenancy, if it is drawn up that way to begin with; and that is fine. However, when a marriage begins to break down and either the wife or the husband can foresee a possible separation, there is no way in which it would be possible for the spouse to get a legal agreement for joint tenancy.
This is just one more reason that we as parliamentarians must continually analyze acts such as the one in question today in order that they are kept current with the living standards and conditions we find ourselves in from time to time. I doubt if there is a member in this House who does not have a current file on his desk expressing concerns of some kind by veterans in his riding. It makes our hearts bleed that when veterans eventually turn to their members for at least an explanation of the situation in which they find themselves, we in many cases are helpless to do anything. Consequently, I fail to see how our motion today can possibly be defeated when it would give us the opportunity, as members, to at least try to support a situation that to me makes common sense.
The leader of the socialists to our left today accused our party of being very hypocritical and claimed he could have voted for the motion had it not contained the word "consider". Let me read the motion as follows:
This House regrets that the government has not extended the March 31, 1974, deadline under the Veterans Land Act and calls upon the government to consider taking immediate steps to extend this deadline.
The leader of the socialists said he could vote for it without that reference to "consider". If he and members of the party to which he belongs were as sincere in their interest for veterans as they make out, and as he so frantically tried to suggest this afternoon, why did not that member, or a member on the government side, stand up and move an amendment leaving out that word? They could then have voted for the motion and, as somebody suggested, saved face.
I have a great deal of respect for the minister. As a matter of fact, I have become acquainted with him as a result of living next door in our apartment house; but if the minister and his government were as sincere as they claim they are in their regard for the veteran, why could they not vote for this motion? This would make the veterans happy and there would not be this so-called hypocrisy, political ploy or game that we are supposed to be playing on this side of the House.

The hon. member for Bruce said that we are playing politics. As I said before, history will prove who is playing politics and it will be shown that it is the government and its coalition cohorts. I am sure the media will understand what is going on here today. I am also sure our some 140,000 veterans will soon understand who is playing politics. The record will be set straight.
I have tried to outline in a very humble way my sincere opinion as a backbencher. Several other backbenchers over here I am sure look at this matter in the same way. I think what the leader of the socialists to my left recorded in Hansard tonight is a disgrace.
